title: RB Jeremiyah Love Press Conference | AZ Cardinals
text: Jeremiah, when you are in college and in the college ranks, you're you're one of the guys, like one of the main guys that are in the room. What's kind of the transition like when you're now in a room of a lot of other guys and established veterans in this league? >> Yeah. Um I'd say it's just like, you know, coming into college as a freshman, you know, I was in the room with a bunch of veterans. Uh I had Audric Estime. Uh Zadarian was a veteran, too. Uh I had Jabrill. Um and D Ford as well. Um Devin Ford. Uh he was a veteran running back from Penn State. Um but it's it's kind of the same, you know. Um I'm coming in as a not necessarily a young guy. Well, young guy to them. Those are guys Those guys are at least 20 23 plus 24 plus. So, young guy in their eyes, but still a pro at the end of the day. You know, we're all pros in the NFL. So, uh mindset was still the same as it always been. Come in, work, do what you got to do, gain the trust of your teammates and coaches. Um but we're at a different level right now in the NFL. So, we're all pros. So, the respect is kind of already there. Um it's just that they know that you're a little younger than them and you know, you got to get adapted to new place. >> Have you been able to lean on the guys of James and Tyler Allgeier and some of the other veterans that are in that room? >> Yeah, yeah, 100%. So, um I've I've talked to James quite a bit, you know. He's a veteran. He's what? Been in the NFL for 10 plus years. Um so, he's got a lot of experience, a lot of wisdom. Um so, I've just talked to him a little bit about, you know, how he takes care of his body, you know, what's his mentality been like throughout all the years he's been in the NFL. And then Tyler, you know, he's been a young bit of a younger guy compared to James. And um So, he's been in well, he's in his second contract. So, um talking to him about how he's maintained his body and uh how he's maintained his mind. So, that's kind of what I've been trying to focus on. Um getting some information about, you know, how you maintain your body, how you go about your day-to-day, and how you keep your mental where it needs to be so you can go out there in every day and do what you got to do. >> You report to uh training camp a month from today. Is there a certain kind of tone you want to set for yourself when camp hits that first day? you know, I want to come into camp, you know, prepared. You know, my body needs to be where I need it to be, you know, as far as from a physical standpoint. And then uh from a mental standpoint, make sure that I've took the time that I needed to make sure that when camp starts it's all about football. You know, that was the time to you know, train, but also, you know, take my mind off the game a little bit. You know, maybe get what, a couple days break, a week break. You know, make sure I'm getting my mental right. And then uh you know, rest of the time this break uh that we have is to train my body to get prepared for training camp. So, uh I'm ready to play actual football. So, um mentality is going to be shoot, all gas, no brakes until the time training camp comes. And when training camp comes, you know, I'm I'm prepared and I'm ready to go. >> What's your goal primarily this season just for you? >> Um just get get better. I want to make sure that I I do what I can for this team to have success. You know, as compared to last year, I want to make sure that we um come together more as a team. Um I feel like last year team was was together. Um but we can also uh but we can always um just become more together throughout throughout the years. Um build a better culture. and then just personally for myself, man, I've learned throughout my time just playing football that uh personal goals aren't going to get you really where you want to get to. It's it's it's all about the team at the end of the day. So, as long as you do your part on the team, usually you'll you'll you'll get the the personal accolades and the personal goals that you have in your mind. So, in my mind, my my goal for myself is to gel really well with this team and and do whatever Coach LaFleur wants me to do. And um just do it to the best of my ability. >> Coach LaFleur called these practices more kind of geared up towards the passers and the pass catchers out there, passing camp. But where have you seen in the 10 practices the most growth in your game? >> I say uh mentally. Physically, just as good as any as any other guy. But I've seen a jump in just my mental. You know, I understand the game a little bit better. You know, being able to you know, see how coach before likes to call this offense and being able to understand why he calls offense the way he calls it. And then also just understand my role as a running back. You know, understand that you know, protections, you know, I got to be at the right place at the right time. Everything is about timing. Protections, you know, blocking. To make make sure that he has a a happy cocoon of love so he [snorts] can do what he got to do, dice the defense up. But um my mental is is is improved greatly throughout just a little bit of time I've been here. And I think it's only just going to get better you know, as we go into training camp and get a little bit right now to you know, maybe get a head start on you know, looking at some teams and stuff like that. But my mental is is definitely gotten a lot better. >> Marvin Harrison was in your shoes just a few years ago being a high draft pick, high profile college player. Have you talked to him at all about just his journey and how he's dealt with the expectations that comes with being in a high in that situation? >> Not much. Haven't talked to him much about that but I've talked to him a little bit, you know, just uh just talking to him man. It's nothing it's never been like oh, what do you do for this? What do you do for that? Or how have you handled this and that? It's kind of just been trying to get to know him more as a person man. I just want to know you know, what do you like to do? You know, outside of the game or you know, how have you shoot, prepared yourself for practice and stuff like that or like how what's what's your mindset where you are right now? So never really talked to him about that deeper stuff but you know, my goal with all my teammates just get to know them more as people because all this ball, you know, we going to jail together where we got to jail together as far as a football standpoint but you know, I want to build connections outside the game. You know, so when when it's all said and done you know, I got guys that shoot I can call on and you know, we can bump heads and and shoot those ideas around with each other or shoot team up to do something or just hang out. You know, I want to be a connection with those guys, but haven't talked to Marv about that type of stuff yet. Um but I would love to in the future, you know, get to pick his brains a little bit about, you know, how he's progressed throughout the years and maybe >> Do you embrace that side of your mind just the the hope and expectations that you bring to this organization or do you try your best to ignore it? >> No, I think about it a lot um because shoot ah this is my future, man. I'm with the Arizona Cardinals for shoot however long I make it, you know. Um if I go out there and perform and do what I got to do then be here for the rest of my career. Um so I do think about the hopes and and expectations that people have for me. Um but I try not to let it weigh in on me too much because at the end of the day um I am who I am and I know I'm going to go out there and do what I got to do and shoot I try not to just let other people influence that that part of me. So um I do think about it uh because it's very important. You know, I've been a lot of trust has been put into me. So I I have I have responsibility to think about it and and do right by uh the people that put their trust in me. So um think about it, but at the same same time still who I am and I'm going to go out there and do my best and hopefully my best is good enough for, you know, my teammates and coaches and the ownership as well. >> Carson, talk to us about the offense. I know you like you said you want to play the role whatever coach wants you to do, but in general just also coming from college, what excites you most about it? >> Um just being in the big leagues like all the pressure is not going to be on me, you know. Uh we got guys like Marv, Trey um and shoot we got a lot of guys in the running back room as well, so we can split some carries if need be, um which I always like. I mean, not you don't need just one guy going out there and getting what 30 carries a game. What we got? 21 games this season potentially? So that's not going to do too good in the long run, but you know, I just love being around guys that are great at football. You know, a lot of professionals around uh NFL and and shoot, it's just it's just great to be around. And I'm excited to just uh you know, showcase our skills together. It's it's been great, you know, in practice seeing guys like Trey and Marvin and shoot, KB and all those guys just do what they do. >> You mentioned that um one of the things you were taught along the way is to [clears throat] not put the personal accolades in front of the team accolades. Was there a specific moment throughout your football career where that that thought process was kind of altered to say like the personal record should be off to the side a little bit? >> Um that's kind of how I've always been. Um never really been the type to uh set like uh well, I've always been the type to set goals for myself, but I they've always been uh connected to the team in some sort of type of way. Like last year, uh I wanted to win the Doak Walker Award in college, wanted to win the Heisman, but those things weren't going to happen unless I did what I had to do for my team and play my role on the team. So, um both of them go hand in hand, so I I I kind of try to make everything team-oriented because at the end of the day it's a team sport. You can't do anything by yourself. Especially as a running back, you got to have a good O-line, got to have a a quarterback that can shoot, read defenses and see a lot of things. Um and you got to have receivers that can take the top off, too, you know, lighten up the box as well. So, um everything goes hand in hand. So, I try not to uh make things personal, make it all team-oriented because if the team is good, shoot, a lot of times you're going to do good as well. >> Carson talked a lot about how you guys have gotten a lot of reps in just since rookie mini camp throughout. Just what's been your early impressions of him and how have you seen that relationship kind of grow? >> Carson's a a great football player and even better person. Played against him in college, uh didn't know much about him. Heard a lot of just different things about him, but getting to learn about him in person and getting to actually see him in person. Yeah, he's a he's a great person and even better football player or vice versa, however you want to put it. Like he's just a great athlete, a great person in general. So, it's been a blessing to be able to uh go out on the field and and take the field with Carson. Um you know, catch some uh footballs and run some routes with him and you know, just build up that chemistry that we're going to need on game day. Uh it's been great. So, uh really looking forward to continuing that in training camp. Uh excited to see uh where he goes and how he excels. but it's been great. yeah, just looking forward to, you know, continuing to play with him. >> We we saw you know, when you got introduced to the to the media how important your family is. With yesterday being Father's Day, what what was that like for you, you know, and and your father as you go to this next chapter in your life and he's been so instrumental in your career? >> Yeah, my mom and dad aren't here right now. So, here by myself. Um but my girlfriend's here. Um but I I uh text my dad happy birthday or happy Father's Day. and that's pretty much it. >> [laughter] >> He's out doing whatever he's doing in St. Louis, probably handling business and probably didn't even take the day off yesterday. So, uh yeah, I did make sure I wished him a happy Father's Day and shoot, I'll bless him with something here uh here pretty soon. >> Like you said, he didn't take the probably didn't take the day off yesterday. What kind of example did he set for you and and and help mold you into the >> Yeah, my my father is a a working man. you could say he's like the backbone of of our family, really. Uh a lot of things go through my dad and uh he takes care of a lot of people. Um and a lot of times, you know, me growing up um shoot, I just saw my dad just, you know, whenever he started something he finished it or whenever he said something he did it. So, word is bond to him. Um he set a lot of great examples of what a man should be, which is, you know, I I wish to aspire to that, you know, as I continue to grow up and become more of a man. Um but I mean, my my my dad was a great role model for me. He still is today. Um so uh I make sure I listen to whatever he says most of the time sometimes you know you don't want to listen to your parents or you want to do it things your own way but I really respect my dad. He is my role model. He is the backbone of my family and shoot a couple years I hope to alleviate him of of some of that pressure and stress that he feels is being you know that man in the family and uh yeah man I'm just going to keep learning from my dad and keep looking up to him and shoot bless him continue to try to bless my family and take care of them. >> You mentioned the offensive line. Just how is that chemistry with you guys and just what do you think of this old line as a whole? >> I think our line is great. A lot of great guys on our line. Uh and the way I've been trying to build chemistry is shoot just just play with them a little bit, you know, try not to keep things always football, you know, sometimes you try to talk to them or you know, make a little jokes at them or shoot I played a game with Paris. so like it's just those little things to try to deepen a get a deeper connection with those guys because those guys without without those guys the offense don't run or the team doesn't run, you know, you can't get you know, those blow you can't have receivers blowing the top off without somebody protecting the quarterback and and shoot I plan to that role as well, you know, I I plan to protect the role and we got to all work together so if we're all more jailed off the field we work better on the field so yeah I I just been trying to do little small things to help better our connection and and build just better relationship with those guys. >> You mentioned the expectation people have said stat makers odds makers whatever that 1200 yards easy first year maybe eight to 10 touchdowns easy your first year. Numbers being what they are what what do you think of numbers and those numbers specifically is it is it foreboding is it bring it on is it yeah I can do that or just watch. Whatever. >> Um as far as numbers man, nothing nothing's ever easy like the way I the way I think of it now is I'm going to have to earn every yard that I get, every touchdown I get. And in college what I scored both years I started I scored 20 plus touchdowns per year and I shoot I haven't seen what that looks like in NFL. I think a lot of guys probably don't score that many touchdowns, but um that's that's the goal that I've set for myself or that's the standard I've set for myself. Um hopefully I can live up to that standard through hard work and dedication and discipline. Um but as far as the numbers man, I try not to think about them or I try not to set specific numbers. Uh so that I'm not trying to I'm not I'm not making it too personal, you know, like I said everything's about the team of you. Make sure you're doing your part on the team like those things will come. Um and the rewards will come and accolades will come and the Pro Bowls will come and all that stuff will come as long as you are keeping everything team oriented and you're playing for your guys. So uh the numbers I try not to set goals for myself, try not to think about them. Um but they're nice to see, you know, if you got a 100-yard game or you or you got uh what a 1,000-yard season like it's always nice to see. Um but those things don't come unless you're doing your job and you're playing your role on the team. So Including that, including that. I would love to um get to that point. I got a lot of time um in between now and hopefully that day I I receive that award. Um a lot of work I got to put in. Um a lot of blood, sweat, and tears got to go into that. So um I would love to be awarded that award. Um but uh as far as right now, I'm just focused on doing what I what I got to do for the team. Um and hopefully down the line that day comes. >> If you're not in the playbook, are you still looking to your comics and you set that up for training camp? Do you have like a reading schedule or how does that work? >> Um so I watch a lot of anime. I read a lot of manga. Um as far as my comic, I pretty much don't do anything um other than nitpick and be like, "I want this to look like this. I want this to look like this. I want this to sound like this." My dad um and the team uh amazing team he's gathered around my comic book, they do pretty much everything for me so I can keep everything football. But if I'm not doing football, um probably just watching anime. Like this this past weekend I was shoot benching some anime. I was uh What was I watching? I was watching um Shoot, That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime, if any of you're familiar with anime. Um it's very popular. Um I watched uh this anime called Re:Zero - Starting Life in Another World. Like I just be benching anime when I'm not doing football um or playing the game. Um But uh I'm I'm involved with my comic but not involved with it, if you understand what I'm trying to say. Like when the final little thing is up, like, "I don't like this. I don't want that to look like that." So that's all my job is. >> Is the anime going to be the the when you take your break, is that mainly what it's going to be focused on or are you going to be able to get away at all? >> Uh I'm not getting away. Like I got to train, man. I got to I got to work every day. Um so my goal is to do something productive every single day, 7 days out of week. Uh and make sure I'm getting better in some type of way and then my little down time watching some anime, play video games, and shoot call it a day.

title: What we learned from OTAs | Atlanta Falcons Offseason Update
text: We welcome you guys back to Ticketmaster Studios. I'm in here with a couple of my friends. I'm Taylor Vismor, DJ Shockley, Tory McElhaney, Dave Archer. We're going to have an off-season update for you guys cuz a lot has happened and there's a lot to talk about as we get ready for training camp. A lot of competition to get to. So, guys, thank you for being here today. Let's just get right into it. Obviously, the biggest competition, the biggest piece coming out of Atlanta that everyone is talking about is the quarterback competition. First open quarterback competition for the Falcons since 2007. Do you even know who those guys were coming in 2007? >> Let me think back. Man, there was one guy. He was incredibly handsome. One guy's name was DJ Shockley. Met that guy [laughter] before. Oh, yeah. Yeah. But no, it brings back good memories. Yeah. Until later until we went to Buffalo. [laughter] I think things went downhill. But yeah, it's crazy what happened here once since that time and that was a fierce battle that I thought I was going to win. But hey. >> But hey, I mean there's >> You were you were going to win it. Okay. Just wanted you to know that. >> Appreciate that, Arch. Thank you. >> Well, let's not let's not look back on 2007. >> [laughter] >> It's 2026 and there's really two guys at the helm of this quarterback competition. Tua Tagovailoa, as everyone knows, signed a one-year deal with the Falcons back in March to go into the 2026 season. And the other guy on the other side of the coin is Michael Penix Jr. who went down in week 11 after a torn ACL injury. Was out for the remainder of the season. And now the big question is who's going to start come September. Kevin Stefanski, the head coach, has made it very clear. We are not handing out a starting quarterback starting quarterback position in in January, in February, in March, in June. It's not happening and there will be a competition until there is no longer one. So, let's talk about Michael Penix first. Like I mentioned, went out week 11 with an ACL injury. What have you seen in his rehab that you've been able to see from him on the field during this OTA's process? >> Obviously, it's going to be a lot of fun, this competition. I think competition breeds the best in guys. I think when sometimes when we get maybe handed a job or you feel like maybe someone's already [music] been given an opportunity, it kind of starts it dulls the knife a little bit if you will. You want that sharpness to you and and competition breeds that kind of stuff. And so we have a true competition here with these two quarterbacks. Michael Penix and Tua Tagovailoa. Starting with Michael as you talked about. I think that Michael has done an incredible job of diving into his piece of the competition, which is kind of competition against himself. How can I get myself back to where I need to be to be able to compete on an even keel with Tua. And that's going to be that's going to be tough. He's got a veteran quarterback coming here that's played a lot of football in the National Football League and been very successful. But what Michael has done is he's he's self-evaluated. I've talked to him a number of times. It's really been cool to hear him talk about some of the things that he wanted to work on, whether it was his footwork, the strength, being able to move, understanding what the pocket presents to him. All that kind of stuff led into what his rehab led into. And I thought that the doctors and the trainers did a really good job of factoring in what it would take to get him up to speed to run Kevin Stefanski's offense, Tommy Rees's offense. And I think he's done an incredible job with that. His attitude has been phenomenal. He's been here every day. I talked to Matt Ryan a number of times about where he thought Michael was. And every time he said, "Man, the dude is the first guy here. He's in the he's in the weight room constantly trying to get himself ready to go. And all that transferred shock to the field when we saw him in OTAs and mini camp, I mean they had him doing drills that I didn't think he would be doing. Stepping over dummies and all that kind of stuff. He essentially did everything. I know they kept him out of 11 on 11, but he was doing kind of the 11 on 11 stuff against air and all it just I think the guy is going to be ready to go, but I just was very impressed with his mindset and how he attacked what he needed to attack. I'll say this, I think to piggyback on what you're talking about, the focus that it takes when you come back from injury. You talked about 2007. I tore my ACL that year, but going into that >> [music] >> training camp, going into that off-season, my mindset was I really have an opportunity to be the guy. [music] And for me, the heightened focus, I think, raised to an all-time high because you knew you had that chance. If you're coming to a season knowing you're the guy, there's a little different feeling. You're still going to work hard, you're still going to make sure that you're doing what you're supposed to, but when you know there's another guy who wants your spot just as bad, the focus you have on the field and off it is is at an all-time high. Now, for for Mike, watching him go through this process, I think, gives him a different mode of how he attacks it. And you got a guy coming in here, Tua, who's on a one-year deal. He's not dumb to the to the to the process of knowing what this league is all about. Tua's coming in here, yeah, he's going to be a great teammate, but he wants to kind of raise his career, too, as well. He's played well, but here he is on a one-year deal saying, "You know what? I got to prove myself to this organization because I want to play more in the National Football League." And then you got Michael Pittman in the same boat saying, "You know what? I want to prove to people that I can play in this league and get back to the level of why you drafted me number eight." So, when you come off an injury, I did it coming into my going into my third year after tearing my ACL, and my biggest thing was I want to get back and I want to compete. I want to show them that I can do all the things I did before so that I could be a part of this team. So, him coming back and having that mindset of, "Yeah, I'm out there doing every drill. I'm in everything." There were moments I I had a chance to talk to him, as well. He talked about there's times he's had to hold himself back. And there's times where he said, "You know what? The staff said, 'You know what? I can't do this, I can't do that.'" But in the moment, "I'm outside. I'm doing scramble drill. I'm running. I'm moving. I'm jumping over bags." Those are all things that I want to show them that I could do. And the fact that you got two guys here who are highly competitive, Two guys who want to kind of take the career to the next step. It's only going to bode well for everybody. I remember going back to college having the same kind of conversation with me and the guy who was there competing every single day in the weight room. I wanted to do more reps than him. I wanted to throw less interceptions. I wanted to complete my passes in practice. All those things that you think are minute in a practice, I wanted to make sure that I was the best at it because we were competing. And ultimately, it makes you a better player. So, I think this situation is going to be the best for this team because both guys, when it comes September, will be ready to rise to the occasion whoever the quarterback may be. They've been going through the gauntlet of making sure they're prepared mentally and physically to be the best they can be for this offense and team. >> Shock, you mentioned that there are times that Michael has mentioned and he's also mentioned it to me that the the training staff and the coaching staff have to pull him back a little. And part of that pulling him back was in team periods, like you mentioned, Arch. But someone who has been playing in team period is Tua. I want to ask you cuz you've been at all these OTAs. You've been at minicamp. You've seen Tua install this offense on at his own time and his own right. What have you seen from Tua, especially in those team periods? >> Yeah, I think that he commands the group really well. I think that he's been incredibly accurate as well, which is something that even Kevin Stefanski talked a lot about coming into OTAs and into minicamp. Is that being kind of something that has been Tua's calling card for a long time is his accuracy. And that's something that I think we're actively seeing from him in these 7-on-7, 11-on-11 periods. He's getting a bit more 11-on-11 reps, obviously, because Michael Penix is not able to go in those. But something that I found really interesting about what the overall goal of OTAs and minicamp is right now, talking to Alex Van Pelt, the new quarterbacks coach, is talking about footwork. And talking about how much everything starts with the feet. If you walk into the Atlanta Falcons quarterback room, there is a sign on top that just says trust your feet. That is such an important part of what the Falcons are attempting to do right now within this competition because as you're talking about Michael Penix is not full go yet. He's not fully cleared yet. So, what can he do? He can work on his footwork. He can work on his timing. He can work on the routes and that's something that even though Tua is having the ability in 11 on 11s to get that work in, it's not that Michael isn't getting that work. Something that Alex Van Pelt said is that there really can't be an a competition until the both parties are fully healthy and ready to go and Michael's not there yet. So, we're seeing a lot of Tua, a lot of that accuracy, a lot of the reps, full team reps going to him and I think he's handled himself very well, but it is one of those things that as we're talking about it and I think you guys can speak to this more than anybody else is that footwork has been such a calling card of what they're actively trying to do in this install because guys, they're going under center. Like I I don't want to like I don't want to overlook that this offense is going to look different in 2026 because there's going to be more under center work. They want to run the ball from under center. They want to be able to do some bootleg stuff. So, when you think about that, Michael Penix has not had a lot of under center reps in the last couple of years by nature of the offense. So, that is a big part of what Alex Van Pelt is wanting to do right now with both of these guys is get them under center, get the footwork right, get the drop backs right, get the timing right and I think that's something that we're seeing collectively from this quarterback conversation through OTAs. >> I think it's funny that we think footwork, you know, and and the layman at home probably thinking well, jeez, I mean footwork, but it's it what Tory's talking about is the reminder. You walk in and and a lot of the stuff we were it was pounded in our head. But you dull to it, you know, you you begin to kind of overlook some of the remedial stuff like Tory's talking about and the footwork is the foundation to everything we do as a quarterback. You know, whether you're doing ball handling, handing the football off, I got to get enough width to get the ball to to Bijan Robinson on the stretch play, or I got to get enough depth to give him an opportunity to do on the counter play. That's just in ball handling. Then the play action, all the stuff, and then mashing your drops up with the depths of routes. But we begin, Shoc, and I know you do the same. We you begin to take that for granted a little bit. But there's the just a subtle reminder. The footwork side. And And when you go in the media, I think it's a great point that Tory brings out. And And getting back to the competition thing real quick, I mean, Joe Montana was one of the great quarterbacks of all time. Um had a chance to be around Joe some. And was at an off-season event, I said, I just happened to walk up to Joe and I said, "Hey, what what are you uh what are you working on in the off-season?" He goes, "Man, I'm I'm just trying to win the job when we get back to camp." I'm thinking, "What?" >> Joe Montana. >> He At the time, he was a two-time [laughter] MVP of the Super Bowl. He goes, "No, my mindset is when I go into the off-season is that I want to I want to win the job. I got to win the job." Now, he did have some competition later on with Steve Young coming in. But to have that mindset and be one of the greatest of all time, that really resonated with me. And I think that that's something that's going on with both of these guys, Tua and Michael, that they they thrive on competition. The most competitive guy I think I've ever been around sits upstairs and is the president of this team now. And he's out there on the field walking around talking to guys. And he's talked to them about that, you know. He's not telling about Hey, you need to run this route. He's not doing that. He's just visiting with guys as to what the mindset is to play this game and play it at the highest possible level. Dude won 125 games in his career. I mean, I think he has a pretty good idea of what it takes to go win and be the best you can possibly be. Kind of cool to have him out there. >> It's been really fun to have Matt Ryan out there. title: The ONE Word That Defines Declan Doyle's Offense
text: in Chicago under Ben Johnson and Declan. We've heard from him. He referred to it as layered counterpunch e, if you will, counter with counterpunches added in, multiple, right? text: Tight end Britain Strange signing an extension. Congratulations first of all. What are your emotions like right now? >> Uh it's really kind of hard to process right now, but it's a blessing. Wasn't really sure how we were going to get there, but it was just about putting your head down every single day, putting one foot in front of the other, and going to work. This is always what I've envisioned, and now it's just time to continue maximizing, and continue becoming the player that I want to become. >> Yeah, what happens now this summer ahead of training camp, and then once you guys get back in the building, the focus is getting ready for this to build on what happened last year, right? >> Right. title: Terrion Arnold's Job Is Not Safe
text: I think, I think there's a pretty intriguing one at corner involving their first round pick from two years ago. And look, this goes all the way back to the combine when Kelvin Shepherd issued his first public challenge Terrion Arnold. And and he told us in and no uncertain time in terms that I just need that kid to be quiet and go play. And look, when maybe the most vocal, most bombastic coordinator in the NFL is telling you you're talking too much, probably time to simmer down and just play some football. And you know, we heard it yesterday from Campbell as well saying that look, when when he gets when he gets out there on the field at full health in training camp, he's he's got to go earn it. And we heard it from Deshaun Townsend who said, "Yeah, you know, he's going to get his job back when he gets out there, but he's got to get back out there first." And I think there's been a level of frustration over the first couple seasons with Terrion's inability to practice in full capacity on a consistent basis even in training camp and then throughout the season. Obviously, injuries last year derailed what should have been, in my eyes, sort of his breakout season. But Campbell was also clear yesterday that the Lions are are done handing out jobs to players whether it be based on pedigree, based on prior performances, based on name. And you know, in his own words he said, "They're not going to let anyone hold them hostage this season." Like if you aren't showing enough Such a great line. If you're not going to let If you're not going to show enough growth or development, and there's someone beneath you that is, like we're not going to hesitate anymore to go to that guy. Because as Campbell put it himself, like it's it's not fair to us. It's not fair to the players. It's not fair to the coaches. Anybody on the roster. And that was clearly a a shift in in his approach to roster construction this year that was informed by their disappointing finish last year. And to be clear, he wasn't talking explicitly or exclusively about TA, but like he might as well have been. That's That's the player along with maybe Mahogany who most fits that description of like, "Yo, it's it's time to It's time to produce." And um you know, he said, "We need to see growth. We need to see development. At some point, you can't wait anymore." And this is a big year for TA. I like that that the coaching staff from Shep to Townsend to Campbell is laying down the gauntlet for him and telling him that if you want to be the guy that you think you are and that we still think you can be, you have to show us. Otherwise, you know, we got NS Reddick straw who's playing a lot with the first team defense in in spring practices because you're not entirely healthy. And we got Rock Ya-Sin who we who we believe in. We even have Cle- Cleil Dorsey who's made a couple plays in camp here. And you know, we're not going to defer to you just because you were a first-round pick 2 years ago. And you know, I Campbell and TA had a a long, occasionally animated conversation coming off the field yesterday before TA spoke with reporters. And TA declined to share what was said between the two of them, although it was mostly Dan talking to TA. And when TA came and spoke with us about obviously the off-field incident, but also just his mindset entering year three, one of the things he said in response to the off-field questions was sometimes it's best to remain silent. So, you know, maybe there's one example of TA taking Shep's advice, also probably his lawyer's advice. But I I when when that scrum ended, the point I want to make here is that I I pulled TA aside cuz he's always willing to talk more. It's one of the things that we all appreciate about him most. And I just said, "Look, man, a lot of these most of these first-round corners that you know, that have been drafted over the past couple years have established themselves as stars in the NFL, Pro Bowlers, all all Pro Bowlers, whether it was Christian Gonzalez in in '23, uh Quinyon Mitchell in '24, two picks before Terion Witherspoon in '23, obviously TA's podcast and buddy and and close friend Pat Surtain. And I asked him, you know, given the way those guys have lived up to their pedigree, is is there a sense that that you want to show this year that you belong in in that conversation? And you know, he he kind of deferred and and said it's not about proving it and went on to to give a very T.A. answer. title: Why Aireontae Ersery is Texans' Most Improved Offensive Player
text: Hey guys, Aaron Wilson. We're talking today about Texans second-year left tackle Tytus Howard. Most of us just call him Tytus. So, Tytus had a successful rookie season. Yes, he experienced some growing pains at the outset, including his matchup with Josh Allen from the Jaguars. And after that game, he had a little mouse under his eye, a little mark, a little um area where he got cut. But, he built some calluses. He built some scar tissue from that game, literally and figuratively. And the next time, he was prepared. And he got better from that game. And that's the big thing, the theme for Tytus and a lot of these second-year players, whether it's a Jayden Peevy or a Jalen Noel, or Tytus, it's about improvement. They drafted him in the second round for a reason. And I got to say this cuz Nick Caserio has rightfully taken some heat. Uh we've been able to, obviously, not just nitpick, but just point out the obvious that Justin Scruggs and Blake Fisher in the second round, that didn't work. But, Tytus, they got this right. In my opinion and many other people's opinion, he is a former Big Ten Offensive Lineman of the Year from the Minnesota Golden Gophers. And to me, he was as advertised, as a good young football player that did a good job of learning from Cole Popovich, taking his teachings to heart, and becoming a better overall lineman. And you know, some of the things that I saw from him, besides the obvious of size and strength and power, was an ability to move his feet, use his hands well, and become a more effective pass blocker. And he's an absolutely pivotal figure for the offense line cuz he protects the blind side of Texans star quarterback C.J. Stroud. So, he's one of the more important players that flies under the radar. And essentially, he has replaced former All-Pro Laremy Tunsil. And he isn't at Tunsil's level yet, but I think there's still more untapped potential with, you know, what he had. Yes, he allowed seven sacks. He had some penalties. But, that was mostly during the start of the season. Where we saw him get better with his confidence to be able to block elite pass rushers. And he's had a lot of growth potential in terms of his conditioning, in terms of everything he's doing to be a better overall football player. And we saw that on display during the minicamp and organized team activities when he was blocking the Danielle Hunters. And Danielle even pointed that out about how much improvement he saw from Tay Sermon. Players, they're very honest. They're not going to praise someone, be over the top about it. And so, Danielle said definitely a lot of improvement. Able to get to spots quicker, shoot his hands, better positioning with his hands, his eyes. He says he goes out there and he's able to execute. And he catches him asking what his pass set was. And very important, he likes the feedback. He says definitely improved. And we heard similar feedback from Cole Popovich and DeMeco Ryans. So, what we're seeing is a better football player overall. And I think that really bodes well for the efficiency of the passing game and also the run blocking. So, when you think about what you're seeing from Ursery, I know offensive line is not necessarily always the first area people think about. People think about the skill players, think about the quarterback, they think about this top-ranked defense. But, Ursery is so critical to the success of this team. They have to have a good year from Ursery, and I think he's primed for that. And so, one of the questions I asked him when I was able to have some time with him was about his game when he had a rough game. And he said he got his butt kicked when he was very accountable about that, the first match up that they lost. And their 0 and 3 start, part of that they didn't get Josh Allen blocked and Josh Allen got a hand on CJ Stroud and they were unable to make that rally that they tried to make in that 2-minute drill. But, you know, he's getting better. So, as he said, you know, he took it on the chin and then got punched in the face. But, the second time he performed well. And a lot of this had to do with the encouragement of his coaches, studying and understand why and this is one of the more efficient pass rushers. A very underrated player, Josh Allen. And he understood it and it was a fun game. And, you know, you see him the confidence and how he's striving to be better and better and be a leader. And as a young player, you know, no he's not perfect. Nobody's perfect as he noted, but he's a certainly a good football player, someone that I think is up-and-coming. He's been through a lot to get to this point. So, let's hear from Tytus Howard right now and then we'll have some more talk from me about this cornerstone of the Texans offense. >> at the early in the season you playing Josh Allen, a real efficient rusher. title: ITB: With Camp One Month Away, What Are The Biggest Storylines Around The Eagles?
text: [music] >> Inside the Birds is back. What's going on everybody? It's Jeff Mosher and I am joined by insidethebirds.com insidethebirds.com's Andrew DiCecco and you know, Andrew and I talked about this. We wanted to do something a little bit different here during what we call the dead period of the NFL and even though Andrew does his DiCecco Daily's and me and Adam have our Inside the Birds series. Right now we're doing the NFC East preview with Greg Cosell. We wanted to put a little break in between and just have Andrew and I kind of discuss training camp which is really only less than a month and a while, about a month away now. And what our biggest question marks or storylines going into camp will be. We now know Andrew that camp will be July 28th and we know that those four weeks go by quickly. We also know that we probably pretty much reached the point where barring something crazy like a Max Crosby trade or Stefon Diggs signs with some team or Keenan Allen that the Eagles like most teams are pretty much set with their roster until whatever happens in camp. So now is a pretty good time to look into it. Are you are you kind of excited about this little exercise that we put together here? >> I am. It was very difficult to whittle it down to just three, but to be clear, these are our three storylines, not necessarily concerns, but something that we are keeping a watchful eye on trending towards training camp. >> Yeah, I like that better, storylines. And so I specifically asked Andrew to send me his three before we recorded, but I didn't send him mine because we just I just wanted to see if there would be some overlap, all right? And and as we record this, Andrew still has no idea what my three storylines are, which makes this more fun and I oddly enough I thought there might be more. There's really one overlap. So, we'll start right now with a storyline that I think our our audience will not be surprised by, but it's very pertinent and and certainly I I didn't even ask you to rank it, but this would be number one for for at least me and probably, you know, you on that if not top two. And that's the health of the offensive line. And as you mentioned in your write-up to me, you know, it even if the offense comes as advertised, if Shawn Marion's a genius, it won't matter, right? If the offensive line isn't A healthy and B effective, right? So, I mean, because they could be healthy as far as passing physicals, as far as not having a specific injury, but if a guy like Landon Dickerson or even Cam with the back, you know, if they're just not the player that they used to be, you wonder, as you wrote Andrew, can can this offense be what it needs to be? Forget about like any any discussion we have about the offense, whether it's Jalen Hurts, whether it's the receivers, the running game, right? Is all going to be an extension of this part of the offense, the offensive line being able to do its job. >> The offense's success is largely predicated on the health of the offensive line. You can have the greatest play caller, you can have the greatest play schemed up in the world, but if you don't have it blocked blocked up properly, it doesn't much matter, right? And I think what we saw last season foundationally as we know, the Eagles want to run the football. They want to set the pace and get Saquon Barkley going and be able to do things off of that. But clearly that wasn't the case last season and I think everything that I've gathered, everything that I've I've seen suggests to me that while the passing game is been the primary focus, I think everything revolves around the running game, Saquon Barkley, and if the offensive line's able to stay healthy, I think the Eagles will continue to be able to to play that bully ball style and control the clock and then you're able to to kind of open things up in the passing game off of that. >> Last year was wonky, Andrew. I've never seen a situation where an offensive line struggled so much in the run game, but really didn't in the pass blocking scenario. Most offensive line will tell you pass protection is harder than running because you're moving backwards. You're in a defensive posture. You're in a vertical set as opposed to a jump set, right? Right from the start. You're running the ball, you get to lean forward, you get to dictate the tempo, and yet the Eagles were so much better at the more difficult part of the blocking in pass pro than they were in the run game. And you know, watching Landon Dickerson and Cam Jurgens really struggled to make angle blocks >> Mhm. >> to to execute the basic motions that were almost second nature to them. I mean, we would watch tape and not You wouldn't even point it out, right? If they made good combo blocks or jumped into the second level because, for I don't know, 10, 15 years, for as long as Stoutland's been the O-line, even going back to Juan Castillo, the Eagles have always ran the ball and and and they read the Eagles ran the ball well and and didn't really have up up and maybe other than like that year where Nick Cole and um and Kyle Shurmur and >> Max Jean Gilles, yeah. >> Yeah, Max Jean Gilles and then later on with Kyle DeVan and then some of the other guys. >> Andrew Gardner, yeah. >> Right, all we've known is an Eagles offensive line that could set the tone. So, last year was really strange in that regard. >> And you mentioned angle blocks. That's going to be imperative that they're able to execute those capably with the wide zone and the the schematic changes that Jeff Stoutland's bringing in, the way the offensive line coach Chris Cooper's teaching it, there was a significant drop-off in Cam Jurgens' play last season. And there's reasons for that. He had off-season back surgery, and that takes quite a bit of time to revert back to your usual form, and he was hindered in his ability to to get to the second level and doing some of the the things that his athletic traits suggest that he should be able to do, that we've seen him do before. So, I think that he is a prime candidate for a bounce-back candidate as long as he's able to stay healthy. And And that the offensive line, the health there is going to be key. That's not even to We haven't even mentioned the depth behind those players, where there leaves a lot There's a lot of questions. It leaves a lot to be desired from an experience standpoint, right? You have Drew Kendall, you have Miles Hinton, you have Jake Majors, Willie Lampkin. You do have Fred Johnson, but there's a lot of questions there. So, who's Who exactly are is would be replacing these players if should they have to leave due to injury? >> Sure. Sure. Something I wonder also, Andrew, is the the intent of Sean Mannion and the wide zone that he's going to bring. And again, we we don't know how No team runs one scheme of run, right? No style of run. It's not like you're never going to see inside zone. It's not like you're never going to see gap or power or the team doing some RPO stuff, too. But there will be some wide zone. Everybody has collectively said that they they're practicing it, so they expect to do it. I wonder if even though that that the they're not doing it with the intention of this, I wonder if a byproduct is making it easier on the health of the O-line because I I had a conversation with Jordan Mailata at the end of last year on on cleanout day. And I was asking him if he felt like the tush push and this just the overly physical style of play that the Eagles have had over the last three or four years, you know, running the ball a lot inside, up the gut, big running backs like Saquon, has also led to a wear and tear on the offensive line that in retrospect makes it seems obvious. And he didn't I expect him to be like, "Nah, not." cuz, you know, offensive lineman especially don't want to like ever relent to that. But, he did say that it could be. He left the door open that their physical brutal style of punishing teams with the inside zone and that and the push play could have taken a toll, which makes sense. They're at the bottom of a pile all time. They're They're They're blocking these massive DTs all the time. So, I do wonder if this style of blocking, wide zone, which is essentially horizontal, I don't want to say that it's not as physically demanding, but I do think moving horizontally as opposed to always up front and instead of blocking a three technique or a zero straight on, you're moving east-west. I wonder if that will take it a little easier on this offensive line and enable them to stay a little healthier. >> Yeah, I'm glad you brought up the what Jordan Mailata had to say when you asked him that, Jeff, because I think going into last season so much was made about how that attrition would affect Saquon Barkley, that style of play, that grinding style where they relied so heavily upon Saquon and the offensive line, how that was going to affect Saquon, but it wasn't taken into account enough about the wear and tear and how that was going to, you know, affect the offensive lineman. And you saw that throughout the season. There were players who made themselves available, but they had to go through quite a bit throughout the week to make themselves available, and they weren't uh nearly at full strength. But, to your point, this new style with the angles and things like that, moving horizontally and stretching teams that way as opposed to being the road graders and and punishing teams and moving forward, I do think that's going to help. And that was really conveyed, whether you're hearing Lane Johnson talk about it at the podium, Cam Jurgens talk about it at the podium. Lane Johnson mentioned that this will be the first time in his career and it's not going to be every time, but he's going to get some guard help. Where if he loses one-on-one, the guard will be there to kind of help back him up there. Cam Jurgens, you could just see how refreshed and and eager they are anticipating this new scheme and how that's going to to help them from just an availability and and a you know, preservation standpoint. >> Sure. And also, and this is the last point I'll make on sort of the blocking scheme element of it. If you go look at the teams that run the Shanahan-McVay style of offenses, um they're constantly kind of going through offensive linemen who are day two, day three guys. I mean, take the Packers, right? Their left tackle for the last few years was Rasheed Walker, a Penn State guy who was a sixth-round pick. And they let him walk. He's now I think he's with the Dolphins. Um they've had they've had Jon Ryan, a backup guard-center having a start at center and guard because their um their first-round pick, whose name is Is it Jordan Morgan? >> Jordan Morgan or El El >> Yeah, Jordan Morgan. I'm sorry. Yeah, I was getting Morgan Moses and Jordan Morgan confused. But But yeah, Morgan, he has not been healthy, right? They've take Elgton Jenkins and they moved him from guard to center to tackle. And then you look at the 49ers, after Trent Williams, they've had just a bunch of guys. Like nobody can really name the center, the guard, the right tackle for the Niners. And the same thing with the Rams. They take They take guys who are oddly shaped, like Alaric Jackson and you know, Steve Avila, right? Third-round pick. Like they These teams that run these offenses seem to intentionally not feel like they need first and second-round picks all over that line because they feel like the scheme itself does the work. So, if I'm Sean McVay, I'm thinking, man, even if I'm not getting peak prime Lane Johnson, peak prime Cam Jurgens, and peak prime Landon Dickerson, even if I'm getting like 70% of them, that's probably better than what some of these other teams are running this scheme with. So, I have a I have to feel like encouraged by that. >> Oh, absolutely. And to add to your point, Jeff, I do believe that with this coach with this coaching staff, you're going to see more cross-training so that you don't leave yourself short-handed. And you I've even seen it a little bit in the spring where there's Sue Kendall getting some opportunities at guard. You know he can play center, but now it's about getting him those reps at guard so that he can be that versatile interior lineman. You Marquel Bell working at left and right tackle. I think that's something that's going to be hugely important. Fred Johnson can play multiple spots. And uh even Miles Hinton, who is a tackle by trade, has been largely working at guard. So, I think you're going to see a lot of that throughout training camp to to better equip this offensive line to to withstand some of those those injuries and have them prepared. >> Absolutely. Uh there's a lot of bodies on this O line, more than I can ever remember. I mean, and and almost all of them are homegrown. A lot of them are day three guys, but nonetheless, they're they're homegrown. There's a lot of work there for Chris Cooper. There's I mean, there's a lot of paint on this easel to work with. It's just, you know, is it is it going to be a Rembrandt or is it going to be a finger painting is is the question with some of these guys. And we'll we'll just have to see. Uh let's go on to your number one because I purposely didn't go with what you're about to mention because I I I figured you might. And also, I want this to be far-reaching our our storylines here. And I had a feeling that out of the discussion of the offensive line, your one your what you have as number one was going to develop. So, I didn't put it. So, your number one, talk about that right now. >> Yeah, it's about how will Jalen Hurts take to this new scheme and how different will it ultimately look? And from my big picture view, Kellen Moore was brought in to implement a lot of the changes that we're expecting to see with Sean Mannion. And for about a month, you saw some of that. I don't think it was fully imagined through his vision, and then they had to scale it back. Turnovers mounted, and the offense just that was not aesthetically pleasing. It wasn't sustainable. And now you're bringing in Sean Mannion to bring in a scheme that you know, at the top of the organization, they they prioritize it. And I think it's something to to to keep an eye on and keep in keep in mind because it seems like this is what they want to do. They're they're rolling with this, and you know, it's kind of the station the the train's at the station. Get on board because it's it's leaving. And so, you look at how that could affect Jalen Hurts. Jalen Hurts, to be clear, has done all of these things before. It's not about that. It's about doing it consistently. And adapting to the changes. And it doesn't seem like they're going to to waver too much from it. Seems like they're really committed to to seeing this through. >> It's going to be really fascinating this year, especially, Andrew, to see certain quarterbacks, Hurts being one of them, sort of adjust to these radical offensive changes that are intended to make the quarterback do something differently than the quarterback has done in the past. Hurts is one. I think the marriage between Justin Herbert and Mike McDaniel is going to be sort of fascinating because what Mike McDaniel does well, and the schemes are supposed to be quarterback friendly, but I don't know that that's always been the way Justin Herbert has operated, right? So, we'll see. Um I think that there was What's the Oh, like Brian Daboll and Cam Ward will be really interesting cuz Cam Ward has such a big arm, but can he use the whole field the way Daboll uh Daboll has worked with these athletic quarterbacks like Dart and Josh Allen, right? Guys who can make second reaction plays and build an offense around that. Ward can run, but he really doesn't, you know, he just he's more of a pocket guy with a big arm. So, I'm sort of fascinated to see that marriage. But, I also think when we talk about Jalen and the Eagles and what to expect, you know, last year Liam Cohen took over the Jaguars and he brought in his he worked under McVay and he brought in his scheme. And if you remember, the Jaguars were really ugly offensively for the first six or seven weeks of the season. Um and it wasn't really until the second half of the year did everything start to really pick up. You know, Thomas started to catch more passes. Parker Washington as a middle of the field guy really evolved to where Lawrence felt really comfortable throwing it to him. You started to see Lawrence use his movement athletic movement more. And I do wonder if that'll be kind of a similar blueprint for how things start with Jalen Hurts. He's got new receivers just like Lawrence had, right? He's got a new scheme. Can he bring his athleticism back into the scheme? I don't know if they're going to be running the ball a lot in a design way with Jalen anymore. But, will there be opportunities for him to pick his spots like when we saw Lawrence run for that touchdown against the Chiefs on the final play of the game when that big upset. I think it was Sunday night or Monday night my game. All this to me makes me wonder because he was have a tough schedule at the start, right? They got like the Rams and the Bears back-to-back. Is it going to be a little ugly early? But, then eventually Jalen, like you said, he's made these throws. Will it eventually become a little bit more comfortable for him? >> Yeah, it's it's it's about consistency and instead of pointing to the Steelers game or the Vikings game, it's about doing it on a week-in, week-out basis. And I think the running game that's going to be at at the crux of everything right here. If the Eagles are able to capably, you know, execute that, I think the the passing games with under center and the play action, everything's going to you're going to see an ideal marriage between the two. And it's more more that they're working on it now and installing it now because if you remember back to last season against the Chargers, they started to implement some of those things. But when you're not doing it in the in training camp and in the spring, it's kind of hard to scrap what you're doing and and adopt a drastically different scheme. So I think Jalen has proven throughout his career that he's willing to embrace change. He's dealt with different position coaches and play callers. But now it's about just really taking to it because it feels to me that the Eagles are fully committed to to implementing this scheme, to take this offense further than where it's gone because I think last season as you saw, it looks like teams caught up to to what they were doing. title: Football at Four: DiCecco's Thursday Eagles Mailbag
text: Now, it is time for Andrew Di Cecco for today's Football at 4 here on The Sports Bash live on 97.3 ESPN. And we have a Andrew Di Cecco mailbag edition of the Football at 4. A lot of great listener questions for Andrew today. A lot of people chiming in all week long with your questions. We appreciate that as always. And Andrew's back to answer them right now on The Sports Bash. Andrew, what's going on, man? >> Mike, I'm doing great. Awesome to be with you. >> As always, July 28th, we now know the birds will be back on the field. They will report and they will be reporting on July 28th, both rookies and veterans. So, we got about a month leading up to that. We'll start our look at the divisions here. But let's get a bunch of these mailbag questions we've been getting for you. And I like this one to start things off. Frank here, who says he's from South Philly, must be down here on vacation. He says, "Andrew, I read your piece on Parks Frazier and Jalen Hurts. It seems like Hurts has a new voice almost every single year. What kind of relationship do these two guys have?" >> Yeah, well, first of all, I appreciate you checking out the story. And you know, these two guys were in the same building last season. But Parks Frazier was the passing game coordinator and now he pivots to quarterbacks coach. So, there's a unique dynamic that needs to be established. And from what I've been able to gather listening to Parks Frazier and and listening to Jalen Hurts' remark about Parks Frazier, I I think it's going to be a a pretty good pairing. Parks Frazier coming in with the background and working, well, he has a background in working with quarterbacks. He's done other things in his career. But for two seasons, he was an assistant quarterbacks coach with the Colts. He mentioned, as I mentioned in the story, he's worked with different quarterbacks, but he's not going to necessarily tailor his approach any particular way despite Jalen having to learn a lot of different coaches in the past and you know it'll be no different. But from what I've been able to to glean in the the past few months, that that relationship is off to a good start, which is obviously encouraging. >> Yeah, and obviously he's had a lot of different offensive coordinators, but we almost don't you know know that he's gone through a lot of different quarterback coaches, too. And you wonder Parks Frazier, is he the kind of guy that can help him kind of you know accelerate the timeline in this new system? >> It's a fair question and I would have to believe so. Parks Frazier, for those who don't know, also spent a season with the Miami Dolphins on their staff as an offensive assistant. So that experience gave insight into the mind of Mike Daniel and how things worked to shape the system ultimately and he was able to discover some things and that gave him a taste of that particular scheme and it kind of I guess piqued his interest. is a fair way to put it and he wanted to add that into you know his coaching rolodex if you will that that that background. So I think that when you're coming in with a with an knowledge and an understanding, at least to a certain degree, it helps facilitate the information and that is going to be imperative as Jalen Hurts looks to take on the different directives and the terminology and even the footwork, which you may not look at it and say that's something that you you often think about, but to be able to sort of uh acquiesce to the scheme, there's going to be certain demands from a mechanical standpoint that have to be taken into account as well. So I think all those things uh bode well for Jalen because of the background that Parks Frazier is coming in with. >> All right, Andrew, let's get another one from Mark in Cherry Hill. He says, "Andrew, do you think Hurts skill set naturally fits a timing-based scheme or is there going to be some serious growing pains this season. >> I don't know if it naturally fits. I don't think that that would be something that I would go with. You know, we haven't seen it in a consistent spurt. We've seen it We've seen glimpses, right? He's done a lot of the things he's going to be asked to do working under center, the play action, throwing over the middle of the field, but it's not about that. It's about the consistency within the the context of this offense and not necessarily always having to go back to what he was able to do in the post season in 2024 or the Vikings game or the Steelers game. Ideally, if you're the Eagles, it's every week. And with this system, timing is paramount. And when you look at some of the the throws that he's largely leaned into, which is outside the numbers, they're very low-risk throws and there's not a lot of traffic there. Now, you could look at it a number of ways and I do believe that the offensive lineman, given their their enormity in size, standing in in the middle of that offensive line probably did, you know, impede his vision a little bit, but there are certain things that you have to do for this offense to be effective. And the ball's got to come out and it's got to come out on time. They've added a lot of interior weapons and Eli Stowers, the tight end, Makai Lemon most notably, who is going to have an early impact on this offense. And if this offense is executed properly, Makai Lemon is the exact type of receiver that you need to be able to move the chains and create some some different matchup mismatches. So, yeah, I mean, we haven't really seen it from J1 on a week in. And well, that's not to say that he can't do it. I think that right there, the ball coming out on time, is going to be one of the the more the more critical aspects of this offense that I'll be keying in on. >> All right, good one. Let's get to uh from Egg Harbor Township. He wants to not me from Egg Harbor Township, a different Mike from Egg Harbor Township. Uh the new offensive line coach, how much of a change is this going to be for guys like Lane Johnson, Landon Dickerson, uh the blocking schemes? They've only worked with Stoutland. >> Quite a bit different. And needless to say, Chris Cooper's coming in with a prior background as a player, so there's that reliability factor, especially when it comes to navigating injuries and and knowing how to press certain buttons with players. text: Welcome into a Friday, June 26 edition of PFTPM. I was thinking about not doing it today, but then I remembered hashtag no days off except when we take days off, but not today. Not today. Maybe next Friday. Next Friday is the third. I think we're already planning to not do next Friday, but this Friday, this Friday, we're here. And one of the reasons we're here is there's stuff that still needs to be discussed. I'm going to begin with Brandon Aayuk. I posted this last night at PFT after we saw two more videos from Brandon Aayuk throughout the day on Thursday. One, he's in an empty closet, but for a backpack that is sitting on a shelf. He goes in and he starts pulling out handfuls of cash, throwing them on the ground, eventually puts a backpack on and walks out. Then later wearing the commander hat, giving out the web address to buy commanders tickets, he's made no bones about his desire to play for the commanders. And I've been saying that the solution for him is simple. He just needs to show up at training camp and they'll cut him because number one, they can't keep him from practicing if he shows up. Number two, when he sets foot on the practice field, if he suffers a season ending injury, they owe him more than $26 million. But I saw someone mention that he's still on the left squad list, and I looked up the 49ers website, and he's not on the roster. He is still on the reserve/left squad list. That is the nuclear option that a team uses when a guy who's already in the building leaves. That's why it's always better to hold out and never show up for training camp than show up and leave. Because once you are there and leave at any point, the team can set in motion a process that results in you being shut down for the entire year. You can't play for anyone, can't be traded, can't be cut. You are locked in until the end of the season. And I looked through the CBA for the rules about the reserve left squad list. And for all the stuff that's in there, there's nothing in there about the reserve left squad list. So, I got in touch with someone who told me it's in the player personnel manual, and I was sent portions of the relevant information as to how this works. He's going to have to petition the league for reinstatement, specifically the commissioner. Now, it should be a fairly basic exercise, but we thought applying for the supplemental draft was a fairly basic exercise, too, until a few days ago. So even though it may be something that has been rubber stamped in the past, not so sure the rubber stamp would be used now because of the stuff that I has been doing. It's just a bad look for everyone. It's a bad look for him. It's a bad look for the 49ers. It's a bad look for the commanders who have been quiet through all of this. It's almost getting to the point where the commanders need to come out and say, "Hey, we're not interested in Brandon Aayuk." if they're not. Until they do, there's a chance they are. But how this would work, he's got to put in the paperwork to petition for reinstatement. The 49ers would then have a 30-day window to evaluate him. Now, part of that evaluation would be put him on the practice field. And when you put him on the practice field, that's when you run the risk of owing him more than $26 million. So they possibly would cut him after he petitions, after he's reinstated, and then after he shows up and says, "I'm here and I'm ready to work because that's when you incur the risk. Otherwise, the only way they owe him anything this year is if he's on the active roster for week one. That's when under the collective bargaining agreement, if you cut him, you owe him his entire salary for the year as termination pay. But, you know, this is a chessboard and there's moves he needs to be making. There's moves he already should have made. He should have petitioned for reinstatement immediately after the season ended. He should have been there for the entirety of the offseason program because all he would have had to do was show up. Hey, I'm ready to work out. Any injury happens that knocks him out for the year. you owe him $26 million. He's done nothing to try to move this in the direction where the 49ers are in checkmate. And the 49ers may end up putting him in checkmate. I was communicating with the general manager today who said, "I'd put him on the suspended list for conduct detrimental to the team." At this point, you can suspend a guy for up to four weeks without pay for conduct detrimental to the team. And then if he continues to engage in conduct detrimental to the team, you can suspend him again. Now, in order to do it right, there needs to be a proper papering of the record. There needs to be letters to the player explaining that you need to stop this, that if this continues, you will be found to have engaged in conduct detrimental to the team. And maybe that's why he deleted the two videos from several weeks ago that attacked the 49ers. and he hasn't directly attacked the 49ers. What he's been doing is cozing up to the commanders and who knows what kind of communications have been happening. But this whole thing seems extremely ill- advised. He's not doing the things he needs to be doing to position himself to be released and he is doing stuff that could make it more complicated for him to get to where he wants to go. And that caused me to raise the question last night on PFT. Is anyone advising him There's there's two simple explanations. He does have an agent. Ryan Williams from Athletes First represents Brandon Aayou. Williams also apparently is part of the management team for 49ers GM John Lynch, which is awkward to say the least. I know they allow that. The union allows that. The league allows it. Doesn't mean it's the best way for business to get done, but that's the situation and it violates no rules. So either Williams has told Brandon Aayuk to do these things that this is how we implement our strategy. If so, it's horrible advice. I think the more likely explanation is he's not been advised to do what he's doing. He's acting against advice.
