title: Lions' Terrion Arnold is arrested, Joey Porter Jr.'s contract situation | PFTPM (FULL) | NFL on NBC
text: Thursday edition of PFTPM, June 25th. Rocketing through the summer already. Before you know it, it'll be the 4th, and as I said yesterday, before you know it, we'll be counting down to week one. I have learned a valuable lesson over the past couple of weeks before we get to the news. I have learned that when And look, I'm not complaining about my job. I know we work in the toy department. I'm I'm not regretting what I've chosen to do with my life. But, there are times where it can be hectic. There are times where it can be demanding. There are times when the stress level is a little more than one or two. And I did myself through those moments by looking forward to the supposed oasis that comes every June and July when PFTPM live is on hiatus, when the news flow trickles. I need to stop doing that. Because every year when I get there, I realize it isn't all that different from the rest of the year. If anything, at times, it's even busier than the rest of the year. But again, I have no official complaints. Although, I guess that means I do. Regardless, here's an example. Last night, settled into the TV room to watch the latest episode, at least as our queue goes, of Widows Bay. Excellent show, by the way. Not on Peacock, not yet at least. Currently on Apple TV Plus. Excellent show. Getting ready to watch it. Uh-oh. Terry on Arnold, Lions cornerback, arrested and to be charged with robbery and kidnapping. This dates back to mid-February, and I remember when I saw the first story. It came from a court hearing involving two individuals who, based on testimony from a detective at this hearing, had some sort of connection to Terrion Arnold. The way the story went initially, there was a house that Arnold had rented in Florida. Someone stole stuff from that house. The two individuals who had been arrested were accused of essentially taking the law into their own hands and trying to recover the stolen property from the suspected thieves. The only problem, as O.J. Simpson once learned, there are certain things you can't do when you're trying to recover property that you believe was stolen from you. And there was enough there, based upon what the detective said in open court, to write a story at PFT pointing out that men with possible ties to Terrion Arnold were arrested and charged with robbery and kidnapping. Now, some of the folks on Twitter didn't react very well to our decision to plant that flag, but the spider sense was telling me then, it's going to be hard for Terrion Arnold to separate himself from this. And as more trickled out in relation to the existing criminal prosecutions of others, that sense got stronger that it's just a matter of time before one of these other players in this broader scheme flipped on Terrion Arnold. And that's what happened on Wednesday. Five total defendants other than him, two of them reached plea deals, and within hours after that, Arnold was finally arrested and will be charged with robbery and kidnapping. Now, he's denied it from the get-go. Last night, a representative for Arnold put out a statement where he categorically denies any involvement and shots were taken at the two individuals, convicted felons I think they were referred to. I hope that's factually accurate for the purposes of the folks who made those statements, but now this has taken on a new level because Arnold is facing these charges. And as the Hillsborough County State Attorney's Office said, the charges carry a potential sentence of life in prison. Obviously, that creates a very significant problem for Terrion Arnold. Creates a problem for the Detroit Lions. For starters, the prosecutors are going to ask that Arnold be jailed until trial starts, citing the allegation that he remains a threat to the community. So, he won't be playing football if that happens and even if he's released on bail, whether it's complete and total freedom, house arrest, something like that, the NFL presumably is going to step in and put him on paid leave. Usually, we see paid leave when there is at the heart of the allegation something involving domestic violence. There have been examples over the years where a player is facing a felony, but is still allowed to play, like Rachaad White most recently in 2024. He was facing felony charges in Texas for street racing. He played until he suffered the knee injury week four, I believe, against the Chargers and that was that for him in 2024. By the time the next season rolled around, the case had been resolved and he had been given a six-game suspension. The NFL looks at all of these situations on a case-by-case basis. They like it that way. They don't want to be bound by precedent. They don't want to have a formula that gets punched into a computer that tells them what to do. And it's all PR driven. How heinous is the alleged crime? How comfortable are we in having this player on the field? They don't view it as punishment to not let a football player play football, which I think is flawed. That was an issue that was litigated between the league and the union 12 years ago when the NFL first came up with the idea of paid leave. This one just seems a little different. Robbery, kidnapping, there were allegations of pistol-whipping and individuals held at gunpoint. If Arnold was the mastermind of the whole thing, and one of the allegations that crystallized yesterday, he called the Largo Police Department and reported the theft. And the contention is within hours after doing that, he orchestrated this scheme to go get the property from the individuals that he believed had stolen it from the house that he was renting in Florida. So, you know, it's not a safe harbor to be the one who presses the buttons and then steps away. If you ordered or and look, I don't know how strong of a word ultimately applies here, but if Arnold's the one who put this in motion, even if he didn't do anything, if this is happening at his behest, his request, his direction, he's got a problem. Obviously, he's got a problem. Even if he's ultimately exonerated, he now is going to have to spend tens if not hundreds of thousands of dollars, go through a full process, unless the case would somehow get dismissed. But, it seems to me that the prosecutors in Florida were very methodical, deliberate, and careful to wait until they had enough to make the charges against Teon Arnold stick. Cuz this all happened in February. February 4th is the date of the alleged incident. So, you charge everyone you think you can charge reasonably, responsibly, correctly. And then when it's time for people to do plea deals, that's when you get the evidence to get the person at the top of the ladder. That's something that happens in a lot of prosecutions. You start at the bottom and you get the individuals at the ground level to flip to someone higher who will flip on someone higher. And my guess is they're going to work on the other three defendants to get them to flip and strengthen the case against Terrion Arnold. So, >> [snorts] >> look, at this point it's impossible to know what's going to happen. Will he be at training camp? Based on what came out last night, I'd be surprised. Will he be available week one when the Lions start the 2026 regular season? He could be, but doesn't look good. So far, it doesn't look good. And I understand, and we all need to understand, he's entitled to all of the constitutional protections, presumption of innocence. He's got to be proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, but it's a serious charge. And it feels like the prosecutor in Florida dotted the i's and crossed the t's before making the move on a player who was a first-round pick of the Detroit Lions back in 2024. So, obviously that's something that we're going to continue to follow as it unfolds over the course of the summer and possibly beyond. All right. Next up, the story of the moment for the NFL continues to be the Brandon Sosbee situation. Quick summary, the NFL didn't just deny his application to be in the supplemental draft, they just said we're not going to have a supplemental draft, which has the practical effect of suspending Brandon Soresby for all of the 2026 season. That was 2 days ago. There has been nothing reported, nothing said, nothing confirmed that Brandon Soresby is going to challenge the NFL's decision in court. Remember, there are two routes. The union could do something about it, but as I said yesterday, the union is in a very delicate spot because Soresby isn't a member. If they have a supplemental draft and Soresby gets picked, someone who's currently a member of the union is going to lose his roster spot. So, I don't think the union's going to do anything. This comes down to whether or not Soresby authorizes Jeffrey Kessler to go to court and to try to get temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, something forcing the NFL to have a supplemental draft. If you're going to do that, if you're going to run into court and sound the alarm that something needs to happen immediately, that someone needs to be ordered to do something, and there's two different types of preliminary injunctions. There's the type that says, "We want the defendant to be told not to do something." The defendant's getting ready to do something, we want that person to be told you can't do it. Then there's the preliminary injunction where you're going to court and you're asking for an immediate order telling a defendant to do something. A mandatory injunction is what they call it in the law. It's usually a little bit harder to get that. You're trying to use the court to force a change in the status quo, not preserve the status quo, force a change in it. That imposes a greater burden on the party that is minding its own business. And is in a position to say, "Hey, if he wants to sue us, he can sue us. But you can't force us to do anything." Here's my point. The clock is ticking. Every day that passes, every hour that passes, it undermines the argument. If you go into court hair on fire saying, "We must have this now. We need an order right now. We need something right now. Move, move, move, move." And you haven't moved on your own to get there, it undermines the point. You need to be acting like it's an emergency if you want to convince a judge that it's an emergency. 48 hours after Brendan Soresby was told there won't be a supplemental draft, no court filing yet. Makes it harder to convince a judge to zip up the black robe and grab the gavel and dispense justice right now. So, let's see what happens between Thursday and Friday. I think if nothing's filed by Friday close of business, he's not going to file a lawsuit. If he does, the NFL would have every right to say, "What the hell took so long to file this thing?" Everybody knew. Now, I know the NFL is trying to act like it was news to them when he applied for the supplemental draft last week, but everybody knew in late April how this was going to go. He's going to try to keep his NCAA eligibility, and if that doesn't work, he's going to enter the supplemental draft. And it shouldn't take all that long to put the paperwork together. Lawyers have pulled all-nighters when needed. When you're getting paid by the hour, you work whenever the work is there. So, if this isn't filed by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Friday, I have a feeling he's not going to challenge the NFL's decision in court. And as I said yesterday, it's probably his best move. He's open to have a long career in the NFL. The NFL is intent on creating that pound of flesh. Having him face some accountability, have some punishment. I do think he needs to sit down sooner than later with someone who will ask him difficult, challenging questions, not a safe space, not softballs, real questions where he provides real answers to try to get this tide of public opinion turned. He really hasn't done anything to make himself into a villain, the circumstances did. And a lot of that was because when he got the court order on June 8th restoring his NCAA eligibility, all these different universities and conferences and commentators just piled on it. And the facts have gotten lost in the sauce. I think it would be in his interest to sit down and tell his story. We need to hear it from him. Why he started betting. We need to hear it from him why he bet on Indiana when he was on the Indiana roster. We need to hear it from him supported by objective facts that once he started playing, he stopped betting on football. Because there's still people out there that view him as a Paul Crewe from The Longest Yard figure, somebody who has thrown games, somebody who has shaved points, and it seems to be a far cry from reality, but the sooner he tells that story, I think the sooner people will understand once he does get into the NFL, he's not going to carry that same stigma that Paul Crewe had when he captained the Mean Machine in both versions of The Longest Yard. So, for now, there's no news, and I think that means there's going to be no lawsuit, and we're not going to see Brendan Soresby connected to the NFL until the scouting combine and then the draft in 2027. Next up, a guy who was drafted in 2023 by the Pittsburgh Steelers. Joey Porter Jr. Gerry Dulac of the Post-Gazette reported yesterday two sides are far apart on a potential extension for Porter. And Porter is in a unique situation. He was essentially a first-round pick in 2023, but he wasn't a first-round pick. That was the year that the Dolphins had given up their first-round pick because of the Sean Payton-Tom Brady tampering investigation. That was the punishment, one of the punishments, for the Dolphins, no first-round pick. So, the Steelers ended up in spot number one at the top of round two, which became spot number 32 overall. The good news for Porter is he's not tied to a fifth-year option. He's entering a contract year. But, like any of the players who get to the back end of a four-year slotted rookie contract, the salary is low. Most of the money is paid early. By the time you get to the end, if you've played well, it's not a number that's even remotely close to what your market value would be. I think Porter is due to make 3.4 million this year, and then next year he'd be eligible for free agency or the franchise tag if the Steelers would use it. And it it highlights a a bigger point as it relates to these contracts. I had someone ask me about it earlier today in the context of Jaylen Carter, who's entering year four. He has a fifth-year option of 27 million plus, but for this year he's in the neighborhood of three or four million. They put the rookie wage scale in place in 2011 to eliminate the reality that there were players every year who were getting this gigantic financial payment and not earning it. The busts were running away with millions that could be redistributed to the veteran players. So, because you can't identify the busts ahead of time, everybody who came into the draft got less. To protect against a bust absconding with money that he never makes, never earns. He makes it, but he doesn't earn Everybody was penalized. Even the players who turn out to be great. And I remember asking Roger Goodell about this when I interviewed him for the one and only PFT Preseason Magazine from 2010, as these ideas were still percolating before the 2011 lockout. What do you do if the idea is we want to keep the busts from making too much money and not earning it? What do you do for the guys who did? Those guys should get second contracts as soon as possible. Now, one of the things that they buried into the 2011 CBA used to be you were eligible for a second contract after two years. As of 2011, you got to put in three. the fair argument is any first-round pick, any draft pick really, that has played at a high level through three NFL seasons, should get a second contract. we need to get away from the well, he signed a contract. He has to honor the contract. The player who is drafted has no say whatsoever in the financial package that he gets. Yeah, there can be some negotiation about cash flow and guarantees and voids, but the money is predetermined. You are paid based upon where you are picked. Your spot, your slot determines your compensation. And it's either take it or leave it. It's not a true contract. None of these contracts are two-way contracts. That's what I'm trying to get people to understand. The team can tear it up whenever it wants. The only thing that protects the player against that is guaranteed structures and cap consequences that force the team to keep the player even if it would say, you know, this guy's probably not living up to what we thought he was going to be. Well, our hands are tied by the remaining guarantees and by the cap consequences of cutting him or trading him. That's the only protection a player gets. The team can tear the contract up at any time. The player is stuck. If the player outperforms, the player is stuck. That's why I think the good organizations take care of the guys who have put in the 3 years and have earned the second contract. Now, it's one thing to say we'd like to give the player a second contract. It's another thing to come to an agreement. And it sounds like Porter and the Steelers are very far apart. And look, they've had a coaching change. Mike Tomlin and Joey Porter Sr. were close. If Tomlin's still there, is there a chance this thing gets worked out? Is there a chance that maybe he helps bridge the gap? He can talk to Porter, he can talk to the team, he can broker a deal. Without Tomlin there, I think that's a lot harder to accomplish. And it could be that he holds in. He wasn't participating in team drills during the offseason program. They've done that with T.J. Watt a couple of times. Where he shows up and he doesn't participate in team drills, doesn't practice until he gets the contract. So, that's one to watch. He could be a hold-in when training camp opens unless they unless they find a way to bridge that gap between what the Steelers are willing to pay and what Porter is looking for. But just remember, just remember, once you have and it's pass-fail. We know it when we see it. A guy who has lived up to his draft standing and a guy who has failed. The guys who fail, they're gone at the first opportunity. The guys who succeed, there's a temptation to ride it out. There's a temptation to take full advantage of the financial benefits of the rookie wage scale. As I've said as it relates to first-rounders who have that fifth-year option, if the team can kick the can through year four, that is a huge savings that that can never be taken away. The Cowboys had Micah Parsons for his fourth year at 3 million. The Vikings had Justin Jefferson for his fourth year in that same range. Ja'Marr Chase in Cincinnati, same idea. That fourth year, if you can get the player who was a first-round pick, who's playing very well, to wait until after year four to demand that second contract, that's that's a huge benefit to the team. All right. Speaking of contracts, I was going to mention this yesterday, but there was too much other stuff to discuss. It hit my radar screen on Tuesday that the Portland Trail Blazers, now owned by former AAF owner Tom Dundon, they signed a new head coach, Mike Dunleavy, long-time Minnesota Timberwolves assistant. They signed him to a contract that guarantees only the first year. It's basically a one-year-at-a-time deal. No buyout if he gets fired after one season. And my first thought when I saw that is, "Don't tell Jerry Jones." My second thought was, "Maybe Jerry Jones already knows." There's a take it or leave it element to rookie contracts. There's a take it or leave it element to coaching contracts. You You think Brian Schottenheimer was in a position to make demands when the Cowboys made him the head coach in 2025? Now, we're never going to know this because they're not going to come out and say it. Would it surprise us to learn that that same structure was used with Schottenheimer? No buyout. We'll guarantee your first season, and then it's one year at a time after that. We decide whether to continue under the terms you agreed to. If you end up going undefeated and winning the Super Bowl, you're stuck unless we decide to change your contract. So, I don't know that Schottenheimer had no guarantees beyond 2025. I wouldn't be surprised if that was the case. And I eventually remembered the Rex Ryan extension when he was entering contract year 2014 with the Jets. And back at the time, there was a sense that it wasn't a good idea to have a coach who was a lame duck. So, Ryan's entering the last year of his deal. He has nothing beyond this season. How does he command the locker room properly when the guys he's talking to are saying, "That guy may be gone anyway after the season." So, he got an extension, but it only guaranteed one year. So, instead of having 2014, he had 2014-2015, and then he had non-guarantees after that. He got fired after 2014 anyway. At least he had a one-year buyout. But in the usual case, if a coach gets fired after the the year of a new contract, he's got multiple years. And that's happened with many coaches over the years. Uh my my point is this, when you consider how competitive it is for head coaching jobs, the supply of capable candidates far outweighs the demand, even in a year where there were 10 openings, which is nearly a third of the league. That's only 10 openings with a lot of qualified and capable candidates out there. I can see NFL teams driving a hard bargain. And if they hadn't already thought of it, this Portland Trail Blazers contract for Mike D'Antoni is going to give them ideas. And it's unfortunate if it happens, but the owners have found a way over the years to And if we ever had access to the actual true and correct information as it relates to what coaches are paid, if we could go back 50 years and see the full data on what players have been paid, the full data on what coaches have been paid, I would submit to you that the rate has increased for players far more dramatically than it has for coaches. Salary cap comes with a salary floor. If you don't have a salary cap for coaches, you also don't have a salary floor. And I've heard stories over the years about specific owners who advocate aggressively to hold down what coaches are getting paid. It's collusion and antitrust violation. No one's going to sue over that. First, you got to prove it or at least you have enough evidence where you think you can prove it. Then you got to be willing to trade in your career as a head coach, as Brian Flores is finding out. I'm surprised Brian Brian Flores still has a a a career as an assistant coach, but you think anybody's going to hire him to be a head coach after he dared to stand up for for and dared to take on the league as it relates to current and historical hiring failures when it comes to race and other issues that Brian Flores is pursuing. Maybe someday someone will do it, but until then the owners have a hell of a lot more leverage than they seem to use when it comes to negotiating contracts with first-time NFL head coaches. They could drive a lot harder bargain. Cuz there's only 32 of those jobs. Especially for a guy like Schottenheimer. I don't want to pick on him, but his circumstances fit this, mainly because he's working for Jerry Jones. Schottenheimer's hip supposedly was coming in 15 years ago. He was well past the window of anybody making him a head coach. And then all of a sudden he gets an opportunity to be the head coach of the Dallas freaking Cowboys? Do you think if Jerry Jones said to him, "Well, you know what? We want you to be our head coach, but we also don't want to have any guarantees beyond this year." What do you think he's going to say? And I'll I'll I'll not be the head coach of the Cowboys. All right, question time. Kristen, fire up the first one from the mailbag. Brandon Elkins. When is the deadline for the finalization of a Super Bowl date in 2028? Does the NFL think it's actually feasible to negotiate for 18 games before the start of the 2027 or the 2026 season to be effective in 2027? I I'm surprised they haven't just gone ahead and locked in February 13th, 2028 for Super Bowl 62 in Atlanta. As I've been reporting throughout the off-season, they specifically haven't picked a date for that Super Bowl holding out hope that the regular season will expand to 18 games by 2027. Earlier this week an interview of NFLPA Executive Director J.C. Tretter with Albert Breer of SI made it clear that the union's not going to do anything anytime soon. Now, is there benefit in moving quickly? You may get a better deal if you move quickly, but I think Tretter understands that it's going to be virtually impossible for him to get the rank and file to vote in favor of 18 games right now. Even if they get a better deal financially by moving to 18 games by 2027, I think it's just going to be hard when it's time to go cast the votes. You're going to have a lot of guys who say, "I don't want to play 18 games. No." They're not going to understand. They're not going to care about the financial benefit of doing what is inevitable cuz it's inevitable they're going to get to 18 games unless the players come 2031 are willing to take a lockout for a full season. They're going to give in on 18 games. And there is wisdom in the idea of let's just go ahead and do it now cuz maybe we can get more if we do it sooner than later. But like I we reported, I don't know, a month, month and a half ago that it's highly unlikely we'll see 18 games by 2027. Still, until they lock in Super Bowl 62, the door is it's just cracked a little bit. It's not quite a jar. I don't know what it takes for a door to be a jar. He's just cracked it a little bit. All right, next question. From Aram. With NFL struggling to get more money out of the TV partners, does the NFLPA have an advantage in negotiating the CBA this summer where they can ask for grass more revenue, give the 18th game in return so the NFL can get more money from their TV partners? I mean, this gets to the point that I was making earlier. And I held back some stuff cuz I vaguely recalled this question was coming. Yes. Yes, there is an advantage in negotiating now. There is an advantage in giving the league the things it's looking for now. The power that the union has when it comes to the NFL, which wants to move now on 18 games in a season, 16 international games, anything else the league is looking for, the power the union has is to say, "Man, not now." Nah, but we're we're we're we're good. And hey, what Tretter told Breer may have just been posturing to get the NFL to come to the table now knowing, "You better be ready to agree to some stuff. If we wait, if you have to wait, we can make you wait. If you want to move now, we want more." So, there is an opportunity there. I just don't know that the union's in a position to take advantage of it when you consider all the turmoil, all the issues, the political reality that I mentioned, trying to get enough members of the rank and file on board. It's a hard sell. It was a hard sell to get the 17. DeMaurice Smith arguably got pushed out because of the CBA extension that resulted in 17 games, even though I believe he understood what was going to happen. They're going to get 17 sooner or later. We may as well agree to it and get better terms now than wait and get lesser terms later. All right, next question. What do we got here? Leedale. You've talked previously about the slim chance of non-US-based teams. How could this work? For example, the franchise tag is likely illegal in Europe thanks to the football ruling on Bosman. I have no idea what that is, but I'll take your word for it. Also, forcing people into a draft may cause problems around all sorts of laws. And hey, that's one of the practical realities of putting a team in a foreign country. But, I look at it this way. When it's time for the NFL to dangle expansion teams to other countries, the NFL will set the terms. The NFL will tell France, England, Germany, wherever. This is what you have to do if you want to have an NFL team. This is what your government needs to do if you want to have an NFL team. You need to change some laws. Here are the laws you need to change. Go change them. Whoever changes the laws first gets the team. The NFL will have that kind of power. We haven't gotten there yet. You know, the only hint of expansion came from Mike Repole, the co-owner of the UFL who just kind of blurted it out a couple of weeks ago that the NFL's talking about expanding by two teams. And when I saw it, I'm thinking, what the hell's he talking about? Nobody's talking about that, but maybe he's privy to some of the talk that hasn't made its way out to the public yet cuz he's got a tie to Tom Brady through their ownership of Noble. Is it Noble? Noble. any issues as it relate to the laws of other countries, the easiest way to fix those issues. It's the same idea as the stadium politics that happened domestically. Where are we going to put the stadium? We're going to put the stadium in whatever state gives us the best deal. Where are we going to put the team? We're going to put the team in whatever country lets us operate that team the way we operate the rest of the teams. And that's the easy argument. Hey, we got to help this team. We're going to have this team. It's going to be a source of local and national pride competing in the National Football League. We can't tie their hands. I'm after the singular goal of these women getting what they deserve and that is the spotlight, that is the the the the the pay, and that is the awareness that and the respect that they deserve for playing this sport. >> OJ, I want to go back to your collegiate career right again, basketball track at Cal Poly. Before I picked up a basketball, I was running around South Central LA with a football in my hand chasing all the boys. We got players in San Diego that were once campers at those teams camps and clinics that are now playing professional football. You're going to need them to step up and support and say, "One, this is legit. Two, it's something that I back." The Olympics are coming to LA, right? In in 2028. You got flag football there. What are you looking most forward to? >> Man, shout out to my girl Kalli Bronson leading the US national team. What I'm looking forward to is US bringing home the gold. That's what I'm looking forward to. The investment that the NFL is putting in, what's happening at colleges and high school, what what Troy Vincent and the team is doing at the NFL offices, just all of that along with what the brands are doing is going to all come together and land on my hometown. I'm a kid from South Central LA, so I'll be there. I'll be supporting, but also exposing all parts of football to the world, whether it's tackle, flag, um just letting everybody know that the girls are here and we ain't going nowhere. So, 2028, we're going to bring home that gold and we're going to see more girls and women playing football than ever before. >> We are so looking forward to that, OJ. And I want to ask you, too, because you guys wear helmets, you wear your uniforms, right? You got all this gear on, but what other ways are you guys able to express your fashion style out on the field, you think? >> Oh, there's nothing like a WNC tunnel fit. I don't Y'all need to check the >> [laughter] >> gram at WNC Football. And that goes for some, you know, players that you see play all over the world. And because of the helmet and the shoulder pads and and the and the uniforms. So, the opportunity that you get pre-game and post-game to show your style and show your fashion, WNC athletes take advantage of. title: DESIGNED CHAOS: Daronte Jones Building Smarter Commanders Defense
text: Washington's defense is faster, but communication will decide everything. >> You are Locked [music] On Commanders, your daily podcast on the Washington Commanders, part of the [music] Locked On Podcast Network, your team every day. >> Welcome inside today's episode of Locked On Commanders. I'm your host, your guy on the ground, David Harrison. And on today's episode, Washington will have to replace Bobby Wagner's command by committee and disguise only works when every defender sells it. But first, speed matters only after communication travels cleanly. We're continuing to run down my notes, observations, and thoughts analysis, all of it from OTAs and Washington Commanders mini camp. And from the defensive side of things, it's become very, very clear that speed is useless if the call travels late. And this isn't just for the Washington Commanders defense, it's really any defense. When you look at the Brian Flores defense that Dorante Jones is coming from, I think you can see a lot of translation there. Now, we know that the Washington Commanders defense is younger this year, it's faster this year. But the question really is whether or not defensive coordinator Dorante Jones can make it smarter, make it more deceptive, and make it better at communicating because that is where the last versions of the Washington Commanders defense that we saw really fell off was their ability to not just communicate, but understand the communication, execute the task within that communication. From what we saw during the OTA period and the three-day mandatory mini camp, I do believe that Dorante Jones is not just installing a new defense, he's upgrading the way that Washington thinks about defense. It's a completely new style of defense because of it. And because of that, this year's defense is going to have a higher ceiling than before due to its speed, its multiplicity, and its ability to disguise. But there is a condition to all of that, to that multiplicity, to that disguise ability, to all that speed, all of it, the upside. the communication has got to continue improving and eventually it'll catch up to the speed that the players are moving at because communication is going to be the backbone of this entire thing. It's going to either hold the defense up or it's going to crumble and the defense is going to come crumbling down with it. A quote that stood out from the OTA period, mandatory mini camp period, uh from Dorante Jones said, quote, "Making sure you have 11 on the field, making sure the guys are lining up right with the right fronts, getting the calls, getting the communication across defensively so everything matters." End quote. And you hear in just in that quote alone, he's not even talking about the execution. He's not even talking about the athleticism. He's not even talking about making the play. He's just talking about getting 11 dudes on the field that are all in the right position, that they're all talking, they all understand what is happening because every part of the defense matters. Every day, as you're going to remember, we've talked about this a lot, that on defense you have to have 11 guys working for one like cause. One dude messes up, one guy slips up, and the entire thing can fall apart. On offense, I think I've used the analogy before if Terry McLaurin slips on his route, the play can still be successful because there are other options. On defense, if you're in say, you know, I mean the the fewer guys you have in coverage, the worse it is. But even if you're saying quarters coverage, one guy slips in his coverage and that could doom the entire play. Jones isn't talking about communication as some generic coach speak phrase, you know, some way to answer a question without answering a question. What he's talking about is the defense that comes before the defense, before the coverage, before the pressure, before the disguise, before anybody gets to run fast, the front has to be right. The call has to get in, the back end has to echo the call, the defense has to know what the offense is showing. Then and only then, after all that's done, once the ball is snapped, the speed can actually become useful. That is the trade-off here. The defense has a higher ceiling than last year's group, undoubtedly, as far as I'm concerned. But it may also have a more dangerous floor because while speed can help fix a lot and mask a lot, it can also expose mistakes faster if the defense doesn't communicate everything they need to communicate properly. And along with that, the team also needs to find its critical leadership voice with Bobby Wagner no longer in the locker room or on the field. And that is the part that I don't think you can just kind of cast away, right? Once it became clear to everybody that Bobby wasn't coming back, you know, through the comments at the combine, etc., through the drafting of Sunny Styles, all this stuff, once it kind of became evident that, you know, and and especially Leo Chanel getting number 54, once all this became evident, it kind of just became It's like, "Okay, boom. There's a There's a line here. Bobby's not coming back. Walk away from it." I don't think it can be looked at that casually. I think Washington, while you you're going to obviously replace Bobby Wagner's snaps into a certain extent, you can even replace his tackle ability, you can replace his production on the field, you're going to get better hopefully in the coverage ability, it can't just like just putting another dude in that position doesn't just replace the authority he brings to the locker room. And honestly, the the authentication, right? The the credibility that it brings the defense. Having Bobby Wagner on the field on your defense brings a level of credibility. Dan Quinn talked about this. He quote, "What we've seen probably more in his communication and ability play calling of of things, the kind of were naturally deferred to Wags." End quote. He was talking about Frankie Louvau, who is obviously a candidate to potentially replace Bobby Wagner and that presence he had on the field because Washington didn't just add speed, it added an element of surprise to counter that offensive thought process using deception, communication, role simplicity, interestingly enough, for such a complex defense, and group ownership of the defensive structure. Frankie Louvau talking to us during the offseason program, said quote, "Every time we're in the room, he, talking about Duron Harmon Jones, talks about us having our thinking caps on, just having that PhD of the playbook, knowing what we're getting the looks, knowing why we're doing it and not just doing things without no reason why we're doing it. And that is one of the biggest things that has really stood out to me during this year's offseason program is players wanting to know the why. But not just players wanting to know the why, coaches delivering the why. It's not just here's your assignment, now go do it. It's here is what the offense is showing. Here is why your leverage matters. Here is why the the guy across from you is showing pressure or whatever they're doing, and here's how all of that stuff ties together, why it's all important. And that is what Daronte Jones is really changing. The way everybody thinks about defense in Washington. Before you even play defense, it's about the philosophy of defense, the mindset of the defense. We used to have the saying in my previous career, slow is smooth, smooth is fast. And what you mean by that when you say that kind of stuff is that by being deliberate, being controlled in your execution, you then get to act faster when it's time to do so because there's no mistake to correct. There's no backtracking to go through on the football field. The translation is it's not about rushing to a guess. Let me make a check just cuz I need to make a check. Guy went in motion, I just need to make a call, and I think this is the right call because I think I memorized the coaching, I think I memorized the meeting, and then from my memory in the meeting, this is the check that I make. No, you have to understand why. Why If if a coach tells you, "Hey, if this receiver, we go from 3 by 1 to 2 by 2 shotgun, running back in the backfield, and it's 3rd and 6, we're going to make this check." Why are we making this check against this team, this quarterback, this offense? If the defender understands why they're doing it, then you have a much better opportunity of remembering and retaining the right thing to do. And you also understand the multitude of checks that you can make, and adjustments you can make, and even if Daronte Jones is on the sideline or wherever he is, and he sees a motion in mind, he goes, "This is the check they should make." And then on the field, they make a different kind of check. As long as the different kind of check still addresses the why of what you're trying to do, and then makes sense, and it fits, it can still be successful. Even Daronte on the side of the field may go, "Okay, not the check that I was going to make, but it still fits the why of what we're doing." It just gives you that much more ability to control what you're doing. So, while the defense is playing faster, it's playing more athletic, it's not going to matter if that speed and athleticism just pulls players out of position even faster than before because nobody understands what's going on on the field. Cornerback Mike said in his quote, "When you embrace your role, understand what you're supposed to be doing out there, doing your job, doing your 1/11th, it makes the game that much more simple." End quote. And that is the really interesting part. A defense that is actually more complex, it's actually more confusing to the offense, and it requires players to know more about it to be able to do more with it is being described as simpler by one of the youngest members of the defense on the team. And yes, Mike said in his quote, he's been known from before he was drafted for his football IQ, but it just shows you what the education process is like. Once the education is in place, the process becomes simple because not only do you understand it, but the players begin to own it. And that is when disguise turns speed into pressure. From watching the practices, from talking to the players, it has become clear to me that the effort this off season is all about alignment, it's all about communication, playing connected rather than just simply being faster and younger. We'll talk about the defense later on this week as one of the major storylines coming out of the offseason program, but for the offense, part of that design now includes more checks, more motions, and this brings up a challenge that goes beyond Jayden, but it's going to serve him just as well. Dan Quinn talking about Jayden said, quote, "He's a multiplier. So, the quickness in and out of the huddles, the motions, the shifts, the communication, the checks at the line of scrimmage, those are all things that are there." End quote. And I love that saying of Jayden Daniels being a multiplier and and David Blough trying to multiply the impact, but it requires more work from not just Jayden. You heard Laremy talk about or we talked about Laremy talking about the offensive line, but also the receivers. Jayden said, quote, "It's asked a lot of them." Talking about his receivers, "with different formations, maybe motions, shifts, things like that, different splits. So, everybody's been there willing to work, wanting to learn, and that's kind of what I've seen from any for everybody." End quote, which is why I'm not troubled by some of the drops we've seen so far uh this offseason as much as some others are. I did an episode on that uh just yesterday. That was our last episode, so if you missed that after this episode, go catch that episode and then I'll go deeper into it there because the guys are thinking about what they're doing more than they're just out there playing fast. You wouldn't move into a house with only the foundation built, right? So, why would I, as an analyst, as a media member, judge an offense or a defense for that matter that's in the same state? This we're just talking about the foundation being built right now. I'm not going to judge the construction of the entire building based on just the foundation. Foundations are incredibly important, don't get me wrong, but this thing is far from even built or from completely built. Even Terry McLaurin is being challenged to do things or to do things he just hasn't been able to do uh, much over the years. By gauging how happy he's been coming off the practice fields though, I think he's enjoying it. Uh, but he's also enjoying the way it's being installed. Terry saying, quote, "Blah does a great job of just explaining his expectations. I think the multitude of formations and route combinations is going to give all of us a flexibility to move around the formation, keep the defenses on their toes, have a lot of routes that may look similar at the stem, but different at the top. And so now we're just trying to hone in on the details of where we need to be to make sure that we're on the same page with the quarterback." End quote. And those motions, shifts, all that communication does is offer opportunities to try and counter the exact type of defenses that Deron Payne Jones is trying to install on the opposite side of the field. DQ saying, quote, "Their ability to get in and out of place quickly." Talking about his offense. "I think that's one. What disguises look like. How can they change a play and get into the next one to give us the best advantage on one particular play. They might have three different plays in their pocket going to the line of scrimmage." End quote. And that to me signals something that I've talked about lately here this off season cuz I think it's going to be a part of the offense, but we haven't really seen it or or gotten a lot of confirmation on it. Kills and cans. You have checks, right? Checks are, you know, tap the helmet, maybe I give you a little thumbs up or a little, you know, hang ten uh, in honor of, you know, Dan Quinn's love of Hawaii and all that stuff. Those are checks, right? We're making small alterations. Kills and cans, right? You hear the quarterbacks say, "Kill, kill." You hear them say, "Can, can." Whatever it is, those are totally new plays. Like we're we're changing everything from protections to to run, to pass, to to routes. Like we're changing everything. I think they're going to have some kills. I think they're going to have some cans and it's going to be really interesting to see as we get deeper into training camp and how the uh, Washington Commanders continue to develop this whole thing. But the next time on Locked On Commanders, we are going to ask whether or not the Commanders already have enough weapons around Jayden Daniels or if they really do need more. Looking back at all my notes again from OTAs and mandatory mini camp. I appreciate you coming back for that episode, coming through for this episode, and any other episodes. And in between them, if you need to find me, you can do so on X at D. Harrison 82, on Instagram on D. Hair at D. Harrison _82, or you can just text me from your handy-dandy cell phone. Become an all-access member of the everydayer club, lockedoncommanders.supercast.com to do that, and you get your first 7 days for free. To the everydayers, as I do everyday, I appreciate you coming through for today's episode, and to everybody, I appreciate you coming through. I appreciate you helping to make Locked On the number one sports podcast network, and until we speak again, if you're out and about, please be safe, please be kind, and I'll see you right back here next time for another episode of Locked On Commanders, part of the Locked On Podcast Network, your team everyday.

title: Commanders Minicamp: Ben Sinnott believes the new offense is 'tight end friendly'
text: You offense, what do you think so far? >> Great, man. I think we got a lot of >> [laughter] >> They always want to talk. Let me restart this. >> Oh, what do you think? Yeah. >> I think the offense is great. I mean, we put in a lot of work since for the last 9 weeks and just uh you know, walk-throughs and you know, going full speed and practicing against each other. I feel like we got a lot more comfortable as time went on and knowing the offense and then, you know, going into um training camp, I think we're going to be more, you know, faster and quicker with everything like that, but I mean, it's been great just marrying everything together, run pass, you know, having the defense on their heels. >> How much of an impact does it make for the running backs when the quarterbacks are under center now? >> Um I mean, a huge impact. Um but I mean, it's a good switch-up under center or or uh I mean, I just think I just think the play-action pass marries a little bit better under center. Um so, you know, defense never know if it's run or pass, you know, as as long as we do our job. >> Right. I mean, we seen what he did as a rookie and you know, um going into his third year and being here with with him for 3 years, I I just see him continue to elevate, continue to be a a leader, continue to feel more comfortable. Um I mean, the talent is there, you know, but uh you know, I just see so much improvement by him and just the willingness to want to win, you know? I think, you you know, going to the to the championship falling short, you know, it just makes him more hungrier. And then, you know, after last year, it's making him more hungrier. So, uh feeling confident with him, and uh I'm excited to see him this year. >> Thanks for the time, man. Do you know what my nickname is for you? >> What's that? >> Third-and-11 machine. >> Let's do it. I love it. [laughter] >> Dude, some of those conversions you had were so outrageous, dude. It's like [laughter] third-and-13, somehow J Max going for 15. >> Yeah. >> It was crazy. >> No doubt. >> Appreciate that. >> Appreciate you. >> Thanks. >> How's it instill? How's the new defense feel? >> It's going well, you know, with web reps come comfortability, and comfortability comes confidence. So, you know, then you just getting the reps, getting the communication, meshing with the guys, and going out there and have fun. >> Fans hear new system, and and fans are like, "Oh my gosh, that that must mean so much." What does it actually mean? Is it just new verbage? >> Man, I always say football is football at the end of the day. Defense is a defense is running the same things, different verbage, you know, different styles when you call stuff, but defense is a defense. Football is football. What do you think of the defense that's kind of coming together out there? With the guys in front of you, Sunny, then you Payne, Kinlaw, like just the unit. >> I think we got a good unit. I think we got a lot of talented guys, a lot of versatile guys, guys we can put in multiple spots. And at the end of the day, you know, we come out of here in about 30 some days, get ready to put the pads on and go out there and have a show. >> What will you do for kind of summer break? >> Come on now, you know what it is. You got to go put in that work. Get ready to put the finishing touches on the machine, and then go out there and have fun. >> Will you stick it it has a does it feel like you're at home cuz Ashburn versus where you actually grew up, solid hour drive, but does it feel home? >> I mean, I kind of always live in my own little world anyway, so it's like at the end of the day, it's it's close enough where I can go home, it's far enough where I still, you know, feel like I'm away from my home, but at the end of the day, whenever I want to go home see my parents, see my mom, my dad, just take that drive up, you know, the toll road, then call it a day. >> Has the ticket request started? >> Nah, they ain't going. They got they They everybody go to Ticketmaster and StubHub and SeatGeek and all them places and go find your tickets. >> Um new offense, first new offense of your NFL career. >> What do you think? >> I love it. Um I think this one really fits my play style and the kind of player that I am and obviously Blough has been great. I mean, you've heard what other guys have been saying and I think everybody's really excited for how multiple will be. They're putting guys in positions to succeed, using guys in a ton of different places. So, I think everybody's really excited about it. It's been fun to learn and and fun to just kind of see how everything's coming together. >> Well, it also seems like the tight ends are going to be on the field a lot more. I imagine the tight end room particularly likes this offense. >> Yeah, you'd hope so for sure. We We've been loving it so far. I mean, just the other day I think in our red zone last red zone day we had five tight ends with touchdowns. So, you'd love to see it and being able to get big bodies out there, create mismatches and we got a ton of talent in this room. So, everyone's kind of a little different. So, like being able to use everybody to their strengths has been really fun to see. >> You mentioned that this offense fits your play style a lot more. Was it ever frustrating for you in the previous offense? >> Um yeah, I think it was definitely frustrating. I've always known what kind of player I was and I'm not blaming it on the offense at all by any means. I've gotten a lot better and I think just the way that it's all structured with this one it just fits my play style more. Play action, outside zone run game. It's kind of more of what I did in college. It's kind of what I'm referring to. >> Yeah, got you. You feel like you could kind of have the breakout that a lot of fans love and so they're they're hoping for it. You feel like that could be this kind of season? >> Yeah, you'd hope so. I'm just kind of focused on day by day and just taking it one step at a time, but really excited uh what I'll be able to do and uh what opportunities I can get. Um so, yeah, really excited about it. >> Thank you, buddy. >> How do you see yourself specifically in >> Just how hungry he is. Like he wants to be great. Like he want like he's listening. Like he come to me every day like, "Oh, what advice you got for me today?" You know, he wants it. >> He's obviously listening because he's reshaped his body and looks in the offseason. Do you take notice of that? >> Come on now. That's that's Alabama. That's us. You know, we working our ass off in Alabama. That's working every day. Every single day he came with that we we ate right. Just protein for lunch and breakfast. There's no carbs for dinner. Supplements every day. Like it's it's a routine that we have to live by. >> You had to have the confidence multiple times to >> What is the most important thing when it comes to the offensive line? >> Yeah, this is my I think this is seventh or eighth playbook that I had. They're damn near all all the same now. It's all the same to me, man. So, I just kind of you know, just trying to take it all in. >> When did you learn all those lessons? Like you were in college and to drop >> This is This is a year later for me, man. It was like again, it was a journey for me. It's a journey. >> To have the just contract stuff resolved and to have the actual security, does that change your approach to the season? Or not change, but like do you feel freer? >> I feel the same, man. You know, I'm thankful for this organization just for them to uh pay me. You know, they they view me as a leader and that's I'm here to do anything they need from me. >> Speaking of being a leader, um this is year number three for Jalen. Have you noticed any type of growth in terms of him being more of a leader? >> Absolutely, dog. Dog, I really don't have to say much about five minutes. >> You learn me uh good food. >> It's simple. >> Um what why was it important for you to come to the first OTA this year since last year? >> Just wanted to get the playbook. Just wanted to get the playbook, you know, get the communication, get the cadence. Being with the guys. You know, I just wanted to come for those two days, show face. Show the coaches that I've been working out, that nothing's dropped off. You know, I'm working. >> You know, what do you mean to you with Jalen? Picture him >> Demeanor. >> I was putting bad things because the guy this year at Syracuse. >> Zay is a dog, man. He always at it. He's a dog. Zay is giving it his all each and every day. I hope y'all can see that. >> You said dog a lot in this press conference, so can you explain dog for all of us? >> Somebody who wants it. Somebody who is dying just to be great each and every day. You know what I'm saying? That's it. That's all That's what I think a dog is. >> Thank you. >> Thanks. Thank you.

title: Wizards President Michael Winger talks 'surreal' opportunity with No. 1 pick in NBA Draft
text: So you've never been a part of a number one pick all your years in hoops. What does this feel like? >> At in the moment it was surreal. It has it has since sort of leveled out into something a little bit more manageable. Um It's a nice position to be in. You're you're not wondering who's going to be picked ahead of you. You're not wondering what type of movement ahead of you is going to occur. Um It's it's it's a peaceful place. >> I bet. I mean everything starts with you. What was it I don't know that you shared this. I've grown up my entire life of bullets Wizards fan and the lottery balls have not always gone our way and in the weeks leading up to the lottery I was saying let's choose optimism. Let's just this is the year it's going to work. Did you hear any of the lottery ball pessimism that existed? Like did you choose optimism? How did you approach it? >> Pragmatism. I certainly I certainly heard all of the negativity all of the pessimism. Um You know but these things are not necessarily connected to the past. You know every moment is sort of it's a new moment. And that's how I felt going into this lottery was this moment is is completely disconnected to any preceding moment. This is its own moment. I feel like we're doing things the right way organizationally. I think I feel like we're doing the right things for the fans. Um and I I I sort of had a feeling that it was going to be a good day for us. I didn't know it was going to be that good of a day. Um but I was pretty optimistic going in that we were going to end up in a good position. >> This may be silly but when I learned that Wall was going to be the representative I was like they're going to get one. Like it's John he was one. Was that at all part of the decision or was that just like a to send John? >> Sure. I mean you know every bit of However you can appeal to the lottery gods to the basketball gods that you do. you don't try to mess with those entities, those deities, whatever. >> Sure. >> Um and you know, John being part of the organization is really special for us. Uh he's on our network. Um he comes around and we're trying to get John back in the fold in more ways than one. And having him on having him on the lottery stage was not necessarily in pursuit of number one, but in pursuit of a special day. And I think that he achieved that for us not only with the outcome, but just by being there. He was there on Mother's Day. You know, and Mother's Day is a special day for him. It's a special day for all of us, but um he chose to be with us on Mother's Day. And that sort of meant something organizationally to us. And I think that uh I think that he and we were rewarded for that. >> Absolutely. You got to make a call. They got to move that from Mother's Day. My wife was not thrilled when I was live streaming that in the car driving to her mom's house. So >> There's a lot of dissatisfied moms. >> Yeah. Um I have been a a vocal and loud supporter of everything you guys have done since you got here. >> Well, thank you. >> It It's what had to be done. You can clearly see it. Like I watch almost every Wiz game. Like you can see the growth with these young guys. How big is this next step? How how big of a deal is the number one overall pick in what you're trying to build a a long-standing perennial playoff contender? >> It is a significant step. Um I don't want to under-sell it, but I also don't want to overstate it. It is it is not the most important thing that will happen. Um the most important thing that will happen is when we graduate from a contender to a champion. Whenever that comes, that will be our biggest moment. Um but you have to build the team capable of getting there. And that requires a combination of veterans, young players, ascendant players, guys who can carry a load, guys who can command the space, who can um police each other, create a culture, and that's what we're trying to build. We're trying to build a legitimate team capable of doing the hardest things that there are that there is to do in the NBA. We have Anthony, we have Trey, we have great young players, Alex, Key, Bilal. I mean, just the group is is terrific. I'm so proud of these guys. But sure, I mean, having the number one pick is it's it's a big responsibility. We have to get that pick right, and it's not just selecting a good player, it's selecting a good player who's also a great ambassador for Washington D.C. And that's hard to do. You have to get to know these guys in a very short period of time. You don't have all the time in the world to to get to know them. You have to make a decision, and you don't get a you don't get a mulligan. >> Right. >> You make the decision, and that's your swing. Like that's that's the swing. You don't get you don't get to you know, get a refund 30 days later if you save your receipt type of thing. And so, we have to get it right. Having the selection is a big is a big deal for us. Getting it right is a big deal for us, and then using that number one pick, whoever that player is, Anthony, Trey, and our young guys, and sort of propel this franchise forward. That's that's the goal. That's the aim. >> How You mentioned Anthony and Trey a few times. We got to see Trey play. We I was at his introductory presser, and you could feel it felt genuine, his excitement to start fresh in D.C. We haven't seen Anthony play, right? Like, how are your conversations with him? How much excitement does he have like Trey did? >> My conversations with AD are delightful. He's a pro's pro. He understands who he is in this league. He understands the direction of the league. He understands what we're trying to do organizationally. He's communicated to me a strong interest in being part of what we're building. >> That's great. Great to hear. >> It is, of course. He, like the rest of us, wants to be on a really, really good basketball team and compete for something big. That's our aim. That's what we want to do, and and I'm delighted that Anthony's here for that. >> How does having vets that are perennial All-Stars, I mean true stars in in Trey and Anthony, how does or does it even impact kind of the direction you want to go with number one? >> It's a great question. Um it impacts it probably doesn't impact the actual selection. Yeah. Um it impacts how that number one pick will likely be developed his first or second year. Um sometimes you just throw guys into the mix and you don't care how many games you win. You don't care if they make a thousand mistakes, you're not going to pull them. Other times if they're playing with, you know, uh high pressure players like Anthony and Trey, they have to make good decisions. They have to make the right decisions. They have to know where to be, when to be, and how to be there. Um so there's it will be probably difficult for Brian Keefe. Um it'll be difficult for the coaching staff to balance the development of the number one pick with the expectation that we're trying to win basketball games. Um but you know, we're development first organization, and so we're going to make sure that we're pouring into this athlete and all of our athletes to make sure that he has the best chance of success in his career while at the same time holding into a very high expectation on the floor and off the floor to contribute to winning and then contribute to our culture. >> With the vets and now adding a number one pick and the young guys like I mean Will Riley like like some the game some of these guys are really starting to show how does the timeline get impacted? Because I think fans like I said earlier like I bought into understanding this is a multi-year thing, right? But does that get accelerated now? >> Not by us. Yeah. And yeah. Not No. Not by us, not by you. Um it gets accelerated to the extent it is accelerated by players. Our players dictate how good we're going to be. Um we are not yet in a position where we will we will um manipulate the roster in pursuit of certain game or season-by-season outcomes. Right now, we are building a roster for the long-term future. If that roster dictates that it's ready to win at a higher level than maybe I perceive them to win, then we'll adjust the roster accordingly and help elevate that group. That's what we did by bringing in Anthony and Trey. if this next season the group sort of uh I don't want to say regresses cuz it's hard to regress on the worst team in the league. but if the team sort of takes a step back in terms of of um our expectations of the team, that's okay. We'll let the team continue to to coalesce and grow. Um but they dictate the timeline. If they're ready to go in I mean you the the Spurs this year, they're really young right? And they're playing exceptional basketball. Um Oklahoma City the year before that, they're really young team. They won the championship. And so young teams can get it done and then other seasons, you know, it it takes old teams to get it done. It's just a season-by-season thing, but we're not going to rush this group. >> And it's fluid, too. I mean to your point like if >> you >> you get to Christmas and it's looking like a playoff team maybe that impacts rather than if you get to Christmas and it's looking like another lottery season. And just allow for the fluidity of it. >> That makes a lot of sense. For the fluidity, your your roster, your caliber your salary cap situation are all embedded with a bit of flexibility and you adjust on the fly. >> Do you want to know something that fans do not comprehend at all? >> Tell me. >> The NBA salary cap. That is that is a complicated mechanism. The aprons and everything else. I I leave that to the experts. But it seems like it's improving. >> reason I have a career in the NBA. [laughter] I'm guessing you don't want to disclose who you're going to draft. >> Probably accurate. >> Okay. But can we talk just about a couple of the players? So I do radio and we get calls from fans and there's probably four camps. The biggest camp is A.J. Dybantsa, the BYU star, okay? Just what do you think of his game? >> Well, if we're going to talk about all these guys, I would tell you that they're all very similar in one regard. They're super talented. this crop of guys at the top of the draft is supremely talented. They would go, you know, two through six in just about any damn draft. Um we'd be lucky to have any of them. They will all develop into great players. They're all great young men. We're going to get a chance to get to know some of these guys here in the next couple weeks. they're highly skilled. They were well coached uh pre-college or well coached in college. They have um an insatiable competitiveness, which is really attractive. Um all have great size. it's just I mean it it's a great great draft to be at the top. >> So, you'll have meetings with all these guys, right? And probably dinners, like some social stuff, some workouts, all of that. Is there Is there one attribute above others that you look for in what you think a number one pick should have? >> That probably is a function of time and place. Um we're in Washington D.C. and so our place matters. Our fan base matters to us. And so we want somebody who can adequately represent our fan base, not necessarily has the same or identical sensibilities, but somebody that when our fans come to the game or tune in to watch, they can they can resonate with that athlete. They say, "That athlete represents me. That athlete is a is a good human being. He takes care of other people. He goes out and he works his butt off every day. Um he has no quit. And so making sure that the guy we select number one is compatible with sort of the just the nature of being in Washington D.C. That's important. Um other than that, they have to be they have to be leaders. It's really hard to be picked that high in a draft um come with the expectations and not be a leader. And guys can lead in different ways. They can lead with their voice, they can lead by example. Um but we look for that. >> How much pressure's going to be on this kid? >> I'd like to reduce it. >> Um and I think I think having guys like Anthony and Trey in the team who've sort of particularly in the case of Anthony who's, you know, been there, done that. this young man doesn't have to come out and score all the points and grab all the rebounds and, you know, dribble the air out of the basketball. We've got guys in the team who can do those things. So, I think for us having having a coach that is really uh really committed to player development and not necessarily go out and win every game right now and, you know, bark and yell at these guys. Um we have a very collaborative head coach. We have a very collaborative coaching staff. Their DNA is development. And then we have guys on the team that can go and ball games. And so, my hope is that there's not a tremendous amount of pressure on this young athlete cuz whoever it is is 19 or 20 years old. I mean, I couldn't handle that pressure at that age. And and most people can't. >> I couldn't. >> And so, you know, a young kid at 19 years old is is very different than that same kid at 26 years old with six or seven years of NBA experience. And so, my hope is that there is that the pressure on that athlete is only self-imposed and not internally or externally imposed. Um and I think that we have exactly the right program and the right current makeup of a team to help a guy like that succeed. >> I I mean, just knowing Keith a little bit and then just knowing everyone's resume in the organizations, like when you talk about the development piece, like you guys have built that. And and I think even the the win-loss ledger might not show it. I think I feel like fans have seen it in some capacity over the years. But, you know, you mentioned the Thunder. You look at this Knicks team in the finals. Trades are also a vital part of the NBA. And being on the right side of those, how active are the phones right now and and how much consideration like getting the number one pick is such a big deal, but maybe it's such a big deal to somebody else. Like how how do you balance all that? >> This is the time of year that phones are ringing regardless of where we would be picking. >> Oops, sorry. I didn't mean to get that. this is the time of year when when when the phones are ringing. It's two weeks before the draft and everyone's trying to figure out what everybody else is trying to do so they can optimize their teams for either the next season or the next handful of seasons. And so we're constantly on the phones. >> I have not yet discovered that having the number one pick increases the volume of calls. It certainly changes the nature of what's discussed. Um fortunately for us the teams that we talk to generally trust us to keep their information quiet. And so they're they're willing to share some interesting things with us. Um but the the volume of calls hasn't increased. The nature of the conversations around one have have been unique. but otherwise yeah, I mean 'tis the season that you know teams are trying to move around either in the draft or move around rosters and some are trying to clear cap space or whatever the case may be. But yeah, the phones ring. >> You can't call about one without a level of seriousness I think. Just because of the importance of all of it. >> That's right. >> Particularly when you would expect to hear on the other end of the phone "Not interested." Right. So you have to make that call and immediately overcome the expectation you're going to hear from the Wizards "Not interested." Um speaking of the expectation of the Wizards, how much do you think you guys have changed the perception around here? >> Of basketball or the Wizards? >> Maybe both or is that separate? >> Uh they may not be separate. Um I think that we've changed what I hear from fans is that while the losing has been difficult and these three seasons have been particularly hard on on the diehards. Um I've heard a level of appreciation for what goes into building a great franchise. I think that a lot of our fans have looked around the league at the sustainable contenders, and they've they've identified those commonalities. We've tried to articulate that we believe in those commonalities, and we're going to ascribe subscribe to those and bring them in house. And for the most part, we've done that. The fans have demonstrated a degree of appreciation, you know, in my outreach to fans. I mean, I'm I walk around my neighborhood or whatever. I get a lot, you know, I love what you guys are doing. Um Now, would somebody who doesn't come up and tell me that they don't? I haven't had that yet, but I'm sure that there's a pretty large population that don't. >> I don't Dude, I think I don't know how long the runway is, but I think by and large fans are behind it.
